activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
story:
Tyson had directed exactly one rehearsal before the fire marshal moved them. The one-act, an adaptation of a story set on the Russian steppe, had been blocked on the thrust stage in the main house, with the audience in a single dark wedge facing the action. Now the sprinkler system in that wing was being repaired, and Mr. Okafor's email said only: "Black box room. Chairs on all four sides. Adapt."

The black box smelled of dust and hot lights. When Tyson arrived, the volunteers had already ringed the playing space with folding chairs, and his three actors stood in the middle looking like people stranded on a grassland, which, he supposed, was what they were playing. Dara, who had the largest part, had her script rolled in one fist. Hector was re-lacing a shoe. Priya was watching Tyson to see what he would do first, and that attention was both flattering and terrifying, the way a crowd's silence beguiles you into believing you belong at a microphone.

"Okay," Tyson said. "Same blocking as yesterday. Top of the play."

They ran it. He sat in one section of chairs and watched, and it was fine. Then he got up, walked a quarter of the way around, sat in the next section, and it was not fine at all. Hector spent the whole first scene with his back to that entire side of the room, delivering the play's best monologue to a wall. Tyson stood, moved to the third section, and watched Priya do the same. Half the audience, at any moment, was looking at shoulder blades. He felt something go friable in his chest, his carefully drawn ground plan from yesterday crumbling like old chalk.

"So that's why the blocking has to change," Priya said, when he stopped them. "It's a stage in the round. Everyone told you?"

"Nobody told me," Tyson said. "I just watched it happen."

He had them run the scene again while he circled the chairs slowly, and the problem began to show him its own logic. The audience sits on all four sides, so no one can face everyone; the director's job is not to make a picture but to keep the actors moving, turning, trading positions, so that no section of chairs only ever sees their backs. It was almost the opposite of what he had practiced. On the thrust stage he had arranged frozen tableaux, composing for a single viewpoint, like a painter. This room wanted something closer to music, a rule about time rather than space.

He tried things. He had Hector walk his monologue in a slow arc. He had Dara and Priya cross and counter-cross, and for ten minutes the stage looked like a traffic intersection, everyone carefully avoiding everyone, until Dara laughed and said, "Tyson, I feel like a migrating bird." He laughed too, and then kept the image. Birds on the steppe. He gave them a reason to move that came from the play itself: the cold wind, the search for a fire, the way people pace when they are frightened for someone. The movement stopped being a solution to the chairs and became behavior, and when it worked, the whole room leaned in.

Still, a question nagged at him all through the water break. Which was more honest, the composed stage that flattered one audience, or the rotating stage that shortchanged everyone a little and no one completely? He asked Priya, because she was the one who read plays for fun. "Is it better to be fair or to be good?" he said. She considered it while unspooling a cough drop. "Depends which chair you're in," she said.

He didn't have an answer, and he noticed he didn't want one yet. He set his notebook on a chair, drew a square with arrows radiating inward, and wrote at the top: nobody's back, no one's whole play. Then he called them back. "From the top," he said. "Dara, when you say the line about the horses, take Hector with you, clockwise." Hector was already moving before the sentence ended, his coat swirling, the lights coming up on all four sides at once.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
story:
Amy had taped the poster to the kitchen door because the kitchen had the best light and, more importantly, the only door her little brother Dex couldn't slam without feeling guilty about the poster. The poster read, in letters she had outlined twice, FROM GENE TO PROTEIN: DECODE IT YOURSELF. Below it was a long string of letters, U C C A U G G G A C U U, and a pile of paper slips with amino acid names on them, which Dex kept rearranging into rude words.

"You said this was a game," Dex said, holding up the slip that read SERINE. "This is homework wearing a costume."

"It's a science fair demo," Amy said. "People walk up, they read the codon chart, they build the protein. It's fun." She said it with the conviction of someone who had not yet watched a single person have fun.

Her mother drifted through with a mug, glanced at the poster, and said, "Looks expensive."

"Cardboard is free, Mom. The only cost was my dignity at the craft store." Actually there had been ribbon, and sticky letters, and a second pack of sticky letters after she'd misjudged the kerning. She had done the math on the drive home, trying to amortize the whole project over the imagined thousands of visitors who would surely come to a county science fair, and concluded that her fixed costs were tragic.

Dex was the test audience because he was home and legally obligated to be nice to her this week, ever since the incident with his skateboard and her calculus textbook, which she had agreed to forgive under diplomatic pressure. He sat at the table now with the codon chart, a grid pairing three-letter mRNA codes with amino acids, and worked his way along the string. "U, C, C," he said, dragging his finger. "Serine. Then C, A, U, histidine. Then G, G, G, glycine." He lined up the slips. Then he hit C, U, U and frowned, because the chart gave him leucine, and he was fairly sure leucine was not a word anyone had ever said out loud on purpose.

"See, this is the problem," he announced. "Your game makes gibberish. Glycine then leucine then whatever. Nobody's body is made of that."

Amy leaned over his shoulder, and the trouble was, he was right. She'd copied the mRNA string from her notes that morning, half awake, and she had never actually decoded it herself. She had trusted the string the way you trust a recipe you've never cooked, which is to say stupidly. She took the chart from him and ran the letters again from the beginning. Serine, histidine, glycine, leucine. Nonsense, at least as far as any protein went, though she had to admit "glycine then leucine" had a nice ring to it, like a law firm.

Then she remembered the girl from the regional fair last year, the one with the beetle display and the terrible posture. They had shared a folding table at lunch, and the girl had picked up Amy's practice problem, decoded from the first letter, gotten garbage, and slid it back with a smirk that Amy had found frankly intransigent. "You started in the wrong place," the girl had said, and nothing else, and Amy had spent the bus ride home resenting her. That was the flashback she kept having, over and over, while she stared at the string: the smirk, the sentence, the refusal to explain. At the time Amy had decided the girl was a menace. Now, squinting at her own poster, she was beginning to suspect the girl had been a gift.

She counted letters. One, two, three, and then A, U, G. She looked it up on the chart, and there it was, and the shape of the whole thing turned over in her head like a mattress. "Translation usually starts at AUG," she said, mostly to the poster. She checked the chart again. "AUG. That's methionine."

"Metho-what?"

"Methionine. It's the amino acid." She pulled the slip from the pile and put it down. Then she read on: G, G, A, glycine. C, U, U, leucine. "So the cell starts reading at AUG, and everything before it is like the instructions on a shampoo bottle nobody follows." She built the rest, slip by slip, and it was a real sequence, one she recognized from her notes, and she laughed, one loud unglamorous syllable, because she had nearly hung a poster on her kitchen door that decoded into gibberish.

Dex changed his mind about the game in the way he changed his mind about everything, instantly and loudly, as if he had never held the previous opinion at all. "Wait, so you have to find the start first? That's actually sneaky. That's a puzzle puzzle." He reset the slips, timed himself finding AUG, and beat his own record twice. Then he ruined the moment by asking if there were prizes.

"No prizes," Amy said. "The prize is knowledge." He made a face of pure, committed hedonism, as though she had offered him a fork to eat soup with, and went to find snacks.

She re-taped the poster, angled so the string was at kid height, and added one line in marker underneath: START WHERE THE CELL STARTS. She looked at it, decided that was too smug, and changed it to FIND THE START. Then Dex came back with cheese crackers, read it upside down from the table, and said, "So every protein starts with the methionine one? Every single one?"

"Usually," Amy said, and then, because it was the honest answer and she wanted to be the kind of person who gave it, "usually," again, more quietly, the marker still in her hand.

He shrugged and reached for the slips. "Okay. Ready, set, methionine."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
story:
I had the whole thing figured out by the time my shift at the pretzel counter started, which should have been my first clue that I was wrong about something. My grandmother had spent the week drilling me for the economics placement exam, because she is a canny old autodidact who taught herself the financial section of the newspaper during long unemployment, and because she claims my degree will be worthless if I can't argue both sides of a rate hike. She was stationed three stores down, at the calendar kiosk she has run since before I was born, radiating disapproval in my direction whenever I checked my phone between customers.

"Stop studying at the register," she called across the aisle during a lull. "It makes you look like you can't count change."

"I'm memorizing the good stuff," I said. "The Fed jacks up interest rates, inflation dies. Eighties. Fixed everything. Everyone should just do that all the time."

She came over without bothering to lock the kiosk, which she would later deny, and stood at the end of my counter with her arms folded, the way she does when she is deciding whether someone is worth correcting. "Everyone," she repeated. "You want to say that sentence out loud one more time, and this time listen to yourself."

I did not listen to myself, obviously. I was eighteen and I had read four articles and one of them had a chart.

"Those rate hikes cooled prices," she said. "I'll grant you that. But you know what else happened that year? I got laid off. A lot of people did. Unemployment went above ten percent during that recession." She picked up a pretzel without asking, salted it with the shaker I was supposed to be rationing, and ate it like it was her prerogative. Which, fine, she'd gotten me the job.

"Ten percent," I said. I did the arithmetic on the receipt paper, because that is what my grandmother has trained me to do since I was nine and overcharged for a churro. "That's one in ten people. Roughly."

"I said above ten percent, and I said roughly nothing. Look it up if you want the exact shame." She dusted salt off her fingers. "My cousin Ray used to say Volcker was a hero. Ray also sold my mother a boat with a hole in it, so consider his judgment."

I told her the exam wouldn't ask about my family's employment history, and she said the exam was run by people who'd never been laid off either, and then a woman wanted a cinnamon twist and our educational seminar paused while I twisted it. The mall was doing its afternoon thaw, the food court filling with people who had come in specifically to be somewhere with air conditioning, and my grandmother retreated to the kiosk to sell a 12-month lighthouse calendar to a man who clearly bought one every year and clearly enjoyed the ritual of pretending to deliberate.

Here is the part I got wrong, and I want to be honest about how wrong. I had been treating the whole thing like a math problem with a clean answer, the kind where you show your work and get full marks. Raise the rates, kill the inflation, collect your A. My grandmother had been treating it like a person, like a year of her life that somebody's tidy policy had walked across in hard shoes. I assumed one of us was doing economics and the other was doing memory, and that the exam would side with me.

It took me until the dinner rush to notice that she was doing economics too, just from the bottom up. She was the variable. She was the ten percent, or she had been, and no chart I'd read had ever drawn her in.

Between customers I texted my study partner, Deshawn, who is also eighteen and also prone to memorizing the heroic version of history. I wrote, "ok so the rate hikes worked on prices but unemployment went over 10 percent in that recession. grandma lived it. how do I argue this Monday?" He wrote back a string of exclamation points and then, "wait THAT'S what we're defending in the debate? oh no." He had been planning to vilify the anti-hike crowd as unserious, which is easier when nobody's grandmother is standing in your mall with a salt shaker and a personal account.

I closed the register at nine and walked her out through the dimming corridor, past the shuttered fountain, her arm hooked through mine the way she likes because she claims the floor is slippery and I know she just likes it.

"So what's your considered position now?" she asked. "You had a position at two o'clock. It was very loud."

"I think it works and it hurts," I said. "I think those are both true at once and I don't know how you choose. I don't know how much hurt buys how much fixing. Nobody in my articles said."

"Hm," she said, which from her is a standing ovation. She stopped by the big glass doors, where the night was still radiating heat back at us, and looked at the parking lot like it was 1982 out there for a second. "Ray's boat, by the way, floated fine. It just leaked." She pushed the door open with her hip. "Come Sunday I'm testing you with flashcards, and this time you're going to get the unemployment number right."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Simon sat in the third row with a notebook open on his knees. Ms. Reyes had assigned ten-minute plays, each drawn from a moment in the playwright's own life, and rehearsal slots began Friday. He had four days and a page of crossed-out lines.

His moment was this: last November, his father had driven four hours to Simon's debate tournament, sat through the semifinal, and said nothing on the drive back except that the heater in the car was acting up. Simon had won. He had expected the win to transmute the silence into something warm, and it hadn't, and he had been chewing on that ever since.

"You're staring at the page like it owes you money," said Priya, dropping into the seat beside him. She had finished her draft on Tuesday, a play about her mothers arguing over whether to sell her grandmother's house. "What have you got?"

"A guy drives. The kid wins. The guy says the heater's acting up. Curtain."

"That's it?"

"That's the whole thing."

Priya tapped her own script against her knee. "Mine's like that too, kind of. My moms fight, and then it just stops. I read it to Deshawn last night and he kept waiting for something. He asked me what changed, and I didn't have an answer."

They walked down to the stage, where Deshawn was taping a rectangle of floor into a playing area. He had taken a theater elective the year before, at his old school, and he talked about it the way some people talked about a place they used to live. When Priya told him Simon's problem, he didn't look up from the tape.

"Aristotle," he said. "In his Poetics, he said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end."

"Meaning what?" Simon asked.

"Meaning your play isn't done. You've got a beginning and a middle. Winning the tournament, the drive, the heater. Where's the end? Something has to be different by the last line, or it's just an anecdote with chairs."

Simon sat on the edge of the stage. "But the real night didn't have an ending. It just had a parking garage and homework."

"Then the real night wasn't a plot," Deshawn said. "That's the assignment. You have to find the ending hiding in the thing that happened." He tore off the tape and smoothed it with his thumb. "Or make one and own it."

Priya flipped through her own script. "So when my moms stop fighting, something has to change because they stopped. Somebody has to say the thing they wouldn't say while they were yelling."

"Or not say it on purpose," Deshawn said. "But on purpose."

Rehearsal came faster than Simon wanted. He cast himself as the father because no one else could sit in silence that long without checking a phone, and Priya played Simon, which meant she got to hold the trophy and glance sideways at a man who kept both hands on the wheel. They ran it in the taped rectangle under the work lights, and the first two minutes were fine, better than fine, and then the heater line came and Priya said it and the play stopped and the auditorium went on being an auditorium.

"That's where it dies," Priya said.

"I know."

"Say something else. Anything."

Simon stayed in the father's chair. He thought about the actual drive, the way his father's jaw had worked, the economist on the radio droning about stagflation, the way his father had reached over and turned the volume down as if the kid in the seat beside him had been a distraction from bad news rather than the good news itself. In the play, the father had not turned the radio down yet. Simon gave him the gesture now, a hand moving toward the dial, and then stopping, and staying there, hovering, while the kid in the passenger seat watched the hand instead of the road.

"Keep that," Priya said from outside the rectangle. "That's the end. The hand."

"His hand doesn't move the rest of the way."

"It doesn't have to. Something changed. We saw it change."

Simon wrote it down. Under it he wrote a question he did not have an answer for, which was whether his father had actually stopped himself that night or whether Simon was inventing a mercy that had never been offered. He couldn't tell anymore. He looked at the line in the notebook, then at the taped rectangle on the floor, and decided that Friday he would find out which one he believed by watching Priya's face when the hand stopped moving.

The sharing session was Friday afternoon, all twelve plays in a row. Priya's went fourth, and at the end her younger self said, quietly, that she wanted to keep the grandmother's piano even if the house went, and both mothers looked at the piano bench that wasn't there, and the lights came down. When Simon's turn came, he took the driver's chair and put both hands on the wheel.

"Ready?" Priya asked, holding the trophy.

"Do it," he said, and reached for the dial.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
story:
The studio smelled of turpentine and old coffee, and the print of Kahlo's "The Broken Column" had been taped to the easel at the front since noon. Megan sat in the second row of folding chairs with her sketchbook open to a page of half-abandoned notes, because the assignment was due Friday and she had promised herself she would stop coasting on the word "powerful" and actually say something about the painting. Her instructor, Renata, had been clear about the method: colour first, then composition, then symbolism, in that order, no biographical gossip until the formal work was done.

"Start with what you can see," Renata said, tapping the nail that pierced Kahlo's painted cheek. "The grey of the corset against the warm landscape behind her. The vertical split down the torso. Anyone want to begin?"

Megan wrote "warm/cool contrast, green belt, red lower half" and then stopped. The boy beside her, Deshawn, raised his hand and started to expatiate on the Ionic column replacing her spine, going on so long about classical architecture that Renata finally cut him off, gently, with a raised palm.

"Save the column. First, Megan, you try. Tell me about the colour."

"It's a desert, but it's not dead," Megan said slowly. "The blues and greens are cool, and they make the red of the lower half and the blood at the corners of her mouth feel louder. The sky is cracked open the way she is." She heard herself and went hot. It sounded like something from a poster. But Renata wrote it on the whiteboard without comment, so Megan supposed it had been acceptable, or at least not wrong.

It was Deshawn, later, scrolling on his phone during the break while they ate pretzels from a shared bag, who found the date. "Wait," he said. "She was eighteen when the accident happened. September 17, 1925. A streetcar crashed into her bus." He turned the phone toward Megan. "The injuries caused her pain for the rest of her life."

Megan looked at the year, then did the arithmetic twice, because it refused to be right. Eighteen. She was eighteen. She had spent the whole afternoon treating the painting like a document from some distant, finished life, and it had begun in a year its painter was the same age as she was now, standing on a street corner maybe, or already seated on the bus, not knowing. The column in the painting was not a symbol she could hold at arm's length with Deshawn's architectural vocabulary. It was a spine.

"You look weird," Deshawn said.

"I'm the same age she was."

"That's not, like, a mystical connection."

"I know it's not." But it changed the critique she had been drafting in her head. She had been planning to write about the tears as symbolic, the nails as symbolic, everything at a safe analytical distance, and now she kept circling back to the fact that the corset in the painting was a real medical corset, the pain a real pain, and she could not decide whether the formal method made that more visible or flattened it. Renata's order, colour then composition then symbolism, assumed you could separate the how from the what. Megan was no longer sure you could, and she was also not sure that her doubt was insight rather than sentiment, the kind of soft feeling Renata had warned them against on the first day when someone called a soup kitchen portrait of indigent men "so brave."

When they reconvened, Renata asked for symbolism. Deshawn talked about the column again, more briefly this time. Then Renata nodded at Megan.

"I don't have a clean answer," Megan said. "The nails and the column read as symbols, but the corset is grey because her actual corset was grey, and once I know that, the colour analysis stops being only about warm and cool. She was my age when it happened. September 17, 1925, a streetcar hit her bus, and her whole life after that, and every painting, came out of those injuries. So the method works, but it also kind of pretends the person isn't in the room." She heard Deshawn exhale beside her, the way he did when he thought someone was being too much.

Renata was quiet for a moment. "You could write the critique as an argument with itself," she said. "That's allowed. A conclusion that admits what it can't settle is stronger than a fake certainty. Most of what passes for confidence in art writing is a reactionary fear of not knowing."

That night Megan sat at her desk with the print Renata had lent her, propped against her lamp, and began a first paragraph about blue sky and split sky, green belt and red cloth, the tears falling in a straight line like the crack, like the column, like a bus route down a street she would never stand on. She wrote for an hour without stopping. Then she picked up her phone and typed a message to Deshawn: did you ever almost get hit by a car and think about it for weeks after. She looked at it for a long time before she sent it, and outside her window a neighbor's dog barked twice at nothing, and somewhere down the block a car door slammed.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
story:
Hudson spread the printout across the kitchen table, weighting its curling corners with a mug, the ketchup, and his mother's reading glasses, which she would want back eventually. The map showed the North Atlantic drawn in ribbons of red and blue, temperature rendered as color, and his task, according to the email from the professor he would not meet until September, was to explain in one page why Britain and Norway sit milder than their latitude deserves. He had two weeks before orientation. He had, he suspected, about four hours of real attention.

His sister Bea dropped into the opposite chair with a bowl of cereal and watched him squint at the page. She was twelve and had recently decided that Hudson, having been accepted to a college she could not yet pronounce, was a person of consequence. "What are the red squiggles," she said, not quite asking.

"Currents," he said. "Warm water moving north."

"Water moves in rivers in the ocean?"

He started to say something about the Gulf Stream and then stopped, because he did not actually know how to answer her without lying. On the page, the red ribbon emerged from the gap between Florida and Cuba, thickened past the Carolinas, and bent east across the whole ocean toward Norway. He had read a number that afternoon and copied it into his notebook, and it had sat there since, refusing to become anything he could picture. About 30 million cubic metres of water per second flowed through that narrow gap, the Florida Straits. He kept reading the sentence and it kept meaning nothing.

Bea leaned over the table, close enough that he could smell the milk on her breath, and he noticed she had brought two bowls. The second one she pushed, without comment, toward his elbow. He ate a few bites of cereal without tasting it, which seemed to satisfy her, and then he stood up so abruptly that she flinched.

"Bathtub," he said. "Don't tell Mom."

He ran the tap hot, plugged the drain, and tore a paper towel into shreds. When the water was deep enough he scattered the shreds along one side and pushed them with the flat of his hand toward the other, watching them bunch and turn. Bea sat on the toilet lid with her bowl, intransigent about leaving, and narrated the paper boats' fate in a low sports-announcer voice. The experiment told him almost nothing except that a bathtub was not an ocean, but something about watching the shreds pile against the far wall shifted the number in his head. Thirty million cubic metres a second through a strait narrower than the bathtub was long, if the bathtub were Florida.

"The book says there's a unit," he said, wringing his sleeve. "One sverdrup. It's named after some oceanographer. So the Florida Straits carry about thirty of them." Bea repeated the word slowly, twice, testing it, then said the Gulf Stream must be very strong, and he said he thought that was one way to put it, and also not the way at all, since strength was not really the point. The point, as far as he could reconstruct it, was transport: heat riding on moving water the way warmth rides on the exhaust of a bus, arriving somewhere it had no business being.

Back at the table, his mother came home with groceries and found her glasses under the syrup. She asked what the wet footprints were about, and Bea said, "Science," with such authority that their mother only raised an eyebrow and started putting away soup. Hudson watched her stack the cans the way she always did, labels forward, and thought about the diagram he would have to draw, the one where warm water reaches latitude sixty and gives itself up to the air, and how the email had asked not for facts but for reasoning, for discernment between possible explanations. That was the word the professor had used. Hudson had looked it up and found the definition circular: the ability to tell good judgment from bad judgment. The trick was that you needed some already.

He wrote his page that evening while Bea did homework beside him, her pencil scratching in a rhythm he found steadying. He wrote that the same sun shone on Labrador and on Ireland, and that latitude alone could not explain the difference, and that the red ribbon on the map carried an amount of water past Florida, thirty million cubic metres every second, that oceanographers called thirty sverdrups, and that this water gave its heat away to the wind on its way northeast, and that therefore the wind arriving in Dublin and Bergen was freighted with warmth from a continent away. Then he sat for a long time with his pen off the paper, because the last sentence he wanted to write was that he could not personally verify any of it, that his evidence was a map, a number, and a bathtub, and that he was choosing to trust the first two. He wrote it anyway. He figured a professor could excoriate him for it or reward him for it, and either way he would learn which kind of professor he had.

At bedtime he passed Bea's door and heard her explaining something to her stuffed whale in a patient, superior tone. "Sverdrups," she was saying. "Thirty of them." Hudson leaned against the hallway wall for a moment, listening. Then he went to his room and turned off the light.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
The chocolate had gone wrong again, and Madison stood over the counter trying to understand what dull gray had to do with anything she'd done. She had melted it carefully, the way the pastry chef's notes said, and cooled it on the marble slab, dragging it back and forth with the scraper until her wrist ached, and still the test stripe she'd painted on parchment dried matte and bent when she snapped at it, like a fingernail instead of a clean break. The kitchen around her was doing its evening work, the sauté line hissing, the dishwasher's racks undulating in and out on their rollers, and none of it cared that she had ruined a third of a kilo of couverture on a Tuesday in July.

"You're overshooting the temperature," Renata had told her that afternoon, without looking up from her tart shells. "Or undershooting. One of the two." Renata's genius was real but came without instruction; she could not explain what her hands knew, and Madison, who had spent four years of high school learning that everything could be broken into steps, found this almost unbearable. She wanted a protocol. She wanted the thing to be knowable the way chemistry was knowable, and instead she had a slab of temperamental sugar and fat that responded to the weather.

Her friend Dev had the same problem in reverse. He texted her a photo from his apartment: a bowl of melted chocolate, a wooden spoon, no marble slab at all, because his kitchen was a hot plate and a windowsill. "How do you even practice without the slab," he'd written, and Madison had started to type back that he couldn't, that the slab was the method, and then she stopped, because she'd been wrong about something recently and it had made her cautious. In June she'd argued with Dev for a whole evening that dessert was trivial, a plutocracy of pleasure where only people who could pay got to care, and he'd sent her a photo the next morning of the cake he'd made for his little sister's birthday, lopsided and perfect, and she'd typed, "Okay. I might have been wrong about that." She was still sorting out what she believed about pleasure and who got access to it, but she no longer assumed the answer was obvious.

So instead of telling Dev it was impossible, she drove to the restaurant early on her day off, when the pastry station was hers, and laid out what she had: a bag of store-bought chocolate bars she'd bought at the corner place, still in their glossy wrappers. She noticed, holding one, that the surface was hard and shiny, that it snapped when she broke off a corner, cleanly, with a sound like a small lock turning. The bars had already been tempered by whoever made them. She stood there turning that over, the way you turn a key in your hand before you know which door it fits.

She melted two thirds of her chopped chocolate in the steel bowl over warm water, took it off, and then stirred in the last third, still chopped, still in its tempered state. She had no idea if this was anything. It might have been a ritual, the kind of thing her grandmother did with salt over the shoulder. But as she stirred, the chopped pieces melted slower than the rest, holding their shape a beat longer, she watched the shards shrink and soften and vanish, and when she painted a stripe on parchment it set within minutes, glossy, and when she bent it, it snapped.

She called Dev from the walk-in hallway, holding the stripe to the light. "I think I found something. You melt most of it, then you stir in the rest still chopped, and it works. No slab." She heard him moving around his apartment. "Wait, wait," he said. "The chopped stuff that's already tempered supplies the crystals. The melted chocolate copies it." Madison looked at the stripe again, at its surface like a dark window. "Seeding," she said. "It has to be called seeding."

They spent forty minutes on the phone while he tried it on his hot plate, his chocolate cooling too fast because his kitchen was cold, then too slow, then seizing slightly when a drop of water got in, and she talked him through each failure like an air traffic controller with one runway. When his stripe finally snapped, he held the phone close so she could hear it, a dry clean crack through the speaker, and they both laughed at nothing.

What she couldn't stop wondering about was the copying itself, the way the melted chocolate took its order from the tempered pieces, as if the example were enough. She thought about her own examples, the teachers and the older line cooks she had quietly patterned herself on, whether she had chosen them or simply been poured into their shape. There was something in that she couldn't quite name, and she was honest enough with herself to admit it stayed blurred. She didn't know if tempering was like people. She only knew the chocolate.

Renata came in at four to start her mise and found Madison still there, stripes of tempered chocolate laid across the parchment like piano keys, one of them broken deliberately, twice, just to hear it again. Renata picked up a piece, snapped it, looked at the clean face of the break, then at Madison. "Where did you learn that," she said. "I didn't," said Madison. "I had a friend without a marble slab." Renata put the piece in her mouth and stood chewing, looking at the rows of stripes, and then she reached for the knife and began chopping the next block, setting a bowl of water on to warm.

story:
The data table had been photocopied so many times that the numbers looked grainy, like something seen through rain, and Violet ran her pencil down the column twice because she did not trust her eyes. The reaction was labeled exothermic, and its K values started high at the low temperatures and then fell, step by step, as the temperature column climbed. She had expected the numbers to rise. Somewhere in her head was the memory of her father saying that heat made everything go faster, and he said it with the certainty of a man who fixed furnaces, and she had never thought to question it until now.

"Am I reading this wrong?" she asked. Dexter leaned over from the next stool, goggles pushed up into his hair, smelling faintly of the chlorine from morning practice. He wanted to be out of the lab by three thirty, because the regional meet started at five and Coach Bryant had promised the anchor leg to whoever showed up ready. He glanced at the page for exactly four seconds.

"That's what it says," he told her. "K gets smaller when it gets hotter. For this one, anyway."

"But the equilibrium constant is supposed to be constant." She said it half as a joke and half as an accusation, as if the table had broken a promise to her personally. Mr. Ferrar had inculcated that idea so thoroughly in September, repeating it at the board with his flat, patient voice, that it had settled into the class like a creed. Constants are constant. He had not said, and perhaps had not wanted to say yet, that a constant could be constant only at a given temperature, that it could be a loyal companion at 25 degrees and a different creature at 50.

Dexter was already packing his bag, but Violet copied the whole table onto a fresh sheet, both columns, and then flipped to the appendix in the back of the text where more tables lived. She found an endothermic reaction there, some dissolution she could barely pronounce, and its K values did the opposite: small and shy in the cold, growing as the temperature rose. She sat with the two sheets side by side like two photographs of the same person taken in different seasons. So heat pushed them in opposite directions. Which one, then, did the reaction want?

She remembered, and did not try to stop remembering, the summer her sister Elise spent teaching swim lessons at the pond. The water was cold in June and the children shrieked and clung to the ladder, and Elise had inculcated confidence in them one shallow step at a time, never carrying anyone, only standing an arm's length away saying you're fine, you're fine, look at you. By August the pond had warmed and the same children flung themselves off the dock without ceremony. Nothing about the children had changed except the water. Violet wondered whether a reaction was like that, whether temperature was not a shove but a change in what the whole system found bearable.

There was a note folded into the margin of her notebook, from Elise, mailed last week from the dorm in Ithaca. Violet opened it again under the lab bench, away from Dexter's hurry. "You asked if college is harder," her sister had written. "It's not harder, it's just that nobody hands you the two tables side by side. You have to go looking for the second one, and half the time you find out you were asking the wrong question, which is somehow the best feeling in the world. Also send socks." Violet had read it six times already and liked it less each time until now, when, holding her two sheets, she finally understood it.

Dexter zipped his bag and paused at her shoulder, drumming his fingers on the bench. "Look, is this going to be on Friday's quiz? Because I have to leave." His want was simple and clean, a starting gun and a lane with his name taped to it, and she envied how little negotiation it required. But she had begun to want something incipient and unnameable, the feeling of two ways of thinking clicking together, her father's furnace logic and the table's cold arithmetic, and she was not ready to leave it half-built.

"Go," she said. "Run fast." She stayed, and she wrote out the whole fact in her own hand at the bottom of the sheet: raising the temperature for an exothermic reaction decreases its equilibrium constant, and raising it for an endothermic reaction increases it. She read it back and felt the click, and then, honest with herself in the emptying room, she wrote one more line beneath it. Why? she wrote, and underlined it twice, and left it there unanswered as the bell rang down the hall and Mr. Ferrar looked up from his desk and said, "Violet, you're going to have to explain to me why the lights are still on in your head."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
The thermometer read 118 degrees and Arianna watched the dark chocolate loosen against the steel bowl's edges, turning from a stubborn block into something glossy and slow. Her mother's double boiler sat on the burner, the water barely whispering below, and beside it lay the marble slab she'd carried home from the restaurant supply store with the last of her graduation money.

She was leaving for college in nine days. The kitchen would be her mother's again in nine days, and her mother did not cook anymore, not really, not since the spring. So Arianna had decided to learn one difficult thing before she went, something that required her hands and her full attention, and tempering chocolate had seemed suitably unreasonable.

The first batch went wrong in a way she hadn't anticipated. She cooled it too fast on the marble, and when she spread it into the molds and waited, the bars set dull instead of shiny, streaked with a pale grey that looked almost like frost. She held one up to the window light and turned it over. It hadn't been like that when she'd poured it.

Her brother Theo came in through the garage door with his soccer bag and dropped it on the tiles. He was fifteen and permanently hungry, and he found the earlier bar she'd left in the car the week before, the one she'd forgotten in the door pocket through two hot afternoons.

"This yours?" He held it out. It had gone soft and reset in the heat, and it wore the same greyish white film, streaky, like something had breathed on it. "It looks like it died."

"It's called fat bloom," Arianna said, reading from the notebook open on the counter, and even as she said it she was turning the two bars side by side and seeing they matched. The chocolate that had melted and reset without her, and the chocolate she had cooled carelessly, both of them wearing the same dull veil. So the streaks weren't a failure of the chocolate itself. They were what happened when it wasn't tempered properly, or when it melted and reset on its own terms instead of hers. She had been treating her ruined batch like a verdict on her ability, and it wasn't. It was information.

"Can I eat it anyway?"

"It's fine to eat. It just looks terrible."

He bit a corner off and shrugged, which was Theo's review of most things. He leaned against the counter and watched her work the second batch across the marble with her offset spatula, spreading it thin and gathering it back, spreading and gathering. Her arm ached. The chocolate needed to come down to 82 before she warmed it gently back to 90, and the thermometer was her only honest friend in the room, telling her things her eyes couldn't.

"You're going to be one of those people who does homework over summer," Theo said. "Revisionist history about yourself. You'll tell everyone you were always diligent."

"I'm going to be one of those people who sends you chocolate that looks expensive."

"That's not a real category of people."

But he stayed, and she let him hold the thermometer while she stirred, and when the chocolate reached its temperature she poured it into the molds and tapped out the air bubbles against the counter, a sound like small applause. They washed the marble slab together in the deep sink, and Theo dried it with a towel that was really a retired t-shirt, and neither of them mentioned that their mother had not come down from her room.

The bars set in the pantry, the coolest dark place in the house, and Arianna made herself wait an hour instead of checking every ten minutes, which took a kind of discipline she suspected she had never previously possessed. When she turned one out of its mold, it came loose with a click. The surface was a clean dark shine, no streaks, no grey, and she snapped a piece off the corner and the sound was crisp and definite, a sound you could hear from across a room.

She put a bar in Theo's hands and one at the bottom of the stairs for her mother, in case she came down before morning. Then she wrapped two more in parchment and set them in the box already half filled with sheets and the desk lamp and the photograph of the three of them from the year before, the year that had turned out to be more fragile than anyone expected. The chocolate would probably bloom in the dorm if the room ran warm, and she knew that now, knew exactly what the grey film would look like and why it would come, and it would still be good underneath the streaks even so.

At the top of the stairs she paused, listening. The bar sat on the fourth step where she'd left it, the wrapper catching the hall light.

"Take it up to her if she's awake," she called down to Theo.

A door opened, soft, somewhere above.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
story:
The line for voter registration wrapped twice around the marble pillars of city hall, which struck Clara as inefficient design for a building meant to encourage participation. She had turned seventeen in April and missed the last election by four months, a fact her brother mentioned at every family dinner with the tenderness of a man tapping a bruise. Today she was registering early, mostly so he would stop, and partly because the youth council had been asked to present a comparison of government systems at the next public meeting, and it seemed dishonest to lecture people about civic machinery she had not yet touched.

The youth council met in a room off the main corridor, between the marriage license office and a vending machine that only accepted exact change. Clara arrived early and spread her materials across the long table: a printout on Westminster-style parliaments, another on separation of powers, and a legal pad where she had written a question she could not yet answer. Her friend Dev arrived with wet hair and a bag of tangerines, dropped into the chair opposite her, and began peeling fruit as if the meeting were already three hours old.

"So what's the actual question," he said, segmenting a tangerine with surgical care.

"Which system is better at getting rid of a bad leader." She turned the legal pad toward him. "Or whether better is even the right frame. In a parliamentary system the head of government isn't elected separately, so the parliament can just withdraw its support. In a presidential system you wait for the term to end, or you go through removal, which needs a supermajority and usually fails."

"Sounds like one of them valorizes speed and the other valorizes stability," Dev said, and she wrote it down before deciding she hated it. valorized speed, she crossed out, then wrote: tradeoff? and underlined it twice, which was her habit when a word was doing more work than it could carry.

The meeting proper began when Priya, the council chair, arrived with the municipal clerk's intern, a graduate student named Marcus who had agreed to fact-check their handouts. Marcus was quiet in the way of people who assume they will be the smartest one in the room and see no need to advertise it. He flipped through Clara's printouts with a pen in his teeth, and at the third page he stopped.

"Where'd you get this example?" he asked.

"The library database. Why."

He turned the page around. Clara had written, in her most confident hand, that no vote of no confidence had ever been decided by a single vote, which she had offered as evidence that parliamentary removals were more deliberate and less arbitrary than they sounded. Marcus did not smile, which somehow made it worse.

"On 28 March 1979," he said, "the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election." He slid the page back to her. "Might want to lead with that instead."

Clara stared at the numbers. One vote. She had spent two weeks building an argument about institutional design, about checks and balances as a kind of architecture, and the whole elegant structure had just been knocked sideways by a margin she could picture as a single person deciding, on a Thursday in March, to walk through a particular door and press a particular button. Dev, who had finished his tangerine, was watching her with the mild delight of a man whose friend has just stepped on a rake.

"So much for deliberation," he said.

"That's not what it means." She was surprised by how sharply it came out. "It means the whole thing runs on majorities, and a majority can be one person wide. That's not a flaw. That's just what it is." She thought of the registration line around the pillars, everyone waiting to be one among thousands, and here was a system where the thousands could come down, in some rotten moment, to one. Whether that was terrifying or beautiful depended on whether you trusted the thousand or the one, and she did not yet know which she trusted, or whether trust was even the right verb for institutions.

Priya called the room to order and asked Clara to present, since the clerk's office had requested a preview before the public meeting. Clara stood with her marked-up printout and did not use the argument she had built. She talked about how a parliament chooses a prime minister from among its own members and can unchoose the same way, and how a president is elected separately and is therefore harder to dislodge, and then she said, "On 28 March 1979, the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election," and let the silence sit for a second, because the numbers did their own work. She told them she had originally gotten the significance backward, and that she was still deciding whether a system that responsive was sturdy or fragile, and that she suspected the answer was both, and that anyone who claimed to know otherwise was probably selling something.

Afterward, while the others stacked chairs, Marcus waited by the vending machine, feeding it coins it kept rejecting. "The removal process in a presidential system exists so that getting rid of a leader isn't just chicanery by the majority," he said. "The threshold's high on purpose."

"And in a parliament it's low on purpose," Clara said. "So which noxious assumption do I like less, that majorities are fickle or that they're right?"

Marcus looked at the machine, which had swallowed his coins and delivered, with visible reluctance, a bag of pretzels he had not selected. He held it out to her.

"You're going to be annoying in college," he said.

She took the pretzels.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
story:
Maelie dragged the whiteboard out of the garage and leaned it against the fence, where the late sun caught the ghost of her father's old grocery lists. At the top she wrote "SUMMER PLAN" and then stopped, marker hovering, because she did not actually have a plan yet. She had a want. In September she would be at college, three states away, and the rowing team held tryouts the second week, and everyone on the forum said the freshmen who showed up having never touched an erg were the ones who quietly disappeared by October.

Her cousin Dev came through the side gate carrying two sports drinks like offerings. "You said six o'clock. It's six forty."

"I was thinking." She uncapped a second marker, a red one, for emphasis she hadn't earned yet. "Okay. So the way I see it, there are two kinds of people who train. There's the kind who goes hard every single day because they think rest is for the weak. And there's the kind who rests so much they never get anywhere."

"Which one am I?"

"You're obstreperous for the first ten minutes and then you're a lawn ornament." She drew a column on the board. "I want to be the third kind. Hard days, easy days, rest days, warm-ups before everything. A whole week laid out before I do any of it."

Dev dropped onto the porch steps. "That sounds like something a person with a laminator would say."

She threw a pinecone at him, and he caught it, which was annoying, and she wrote "MON: hard" and then, after a pause, "TUES: rest." The rest days looked strange on the board, like admitting defeat in advance, but the forum threads she'd read half the night kept repeating the same word: recovery. She wasn't sure she believed in it yet. Believing would have to wait for evidence.

Monday she did the hardest workout of her life, or the hardest she could invent in a backyard: squat jumps, burpees, lunges down the length of the fence, a plank held until her arms shook like the clothesline in wind. Dev counted repetitions with theatrical gravitas, announcing each round like a boxing announcer, and when she finished she felt, against all expectation, wonderful. Untouched. She jogged a victory lap around the birdbath and went inside for dinner feeling faintly immortal.

Tuesday she kept the rest day, though it cost her something to sit still. Wednesday morning she woke and her legs worked fine, and she thought the plan was already a success, and she was smug about it all through breakfast. Wednesday afternoon, climbing the porch steps, she stopped halfway up because her thighs had turned to something alien, swollen and screaming. Thursday was worse. She walked from the back door to the whiteboard like a woman twice her age, lowering herself onto the steps with both hands.

"Okay," she said when Dev arrived, "the soreness came late. Like really late. I felt great the day of, fine the next morning, and now it's day three and I can barely get down these steps."

Dev looked at her with the pity of someone who had never once had a plan. "So your body is two days behind your brain."

"Two, three. Somewhere in there." She picked up the marker, wrote at the bottom of the board, and read it aloud so he could check it against his own memory of her week. "If a workout is new or really intense, the worst soreness doesn't show up right away. It peaks twenty-four to seventy-two hours after." She underlined nothing. The sentence sat there, plain as a grocery list, and it explained her legs better than any feeling had. The problem, she realized, was that her whole plan had been built on how she felt immediately after each day, and her body kept a slower clock than that. She moved the Thursday session to Saturday. She wrote "warm-up" before every line that had exercise in it, then stood back.

"So it's not that you were wrong," Dev said. "You were just early."

"Or late. I genuinely can't tell which." She looked at the board, at the week she had argued her way into, half science and half guess. Saturday was still a guess. Whether the rest days were enough, whether the whole thing would hold up in September, all of it stayed open, and she found she could live with that more easily than she'd expected. She handed him the red marker. "Write your name under 'spotter.' If I sue you over these steps, my mom says the family can't indemnify you."

"You'd sue me."

"I'd limp at you very dramatically." She got up off the steps, slowly, one hand on the rail, and started her warm-up.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
story:
The photo arrived in Alice's phone at 4:12 in the afternoon: a flooded underpass, brown water swallowing a stalled sedan, a man on a roof holding a hand-lettered sign that read THEY LET THIS HAPPEN. Her grandmother had sent it to the whole family thread with the message "Everyone in town needs to see this before the meeting tonight," and then, a minute later, "Alice, forward this to your friends." The council meeting started at seven. Three hours, and already her aunt had replied with a string of angry faces.

She was at Priya's house, the two of them sprawled on the kitchen floor around a laptop, supposedly working on a shared college application essay that had stalled somewhere around the second paragraph. Alice held up her phone. "My grandma wants me to spread this. And I kind of want to. Look at it. If that's the Willow Street underpass from last month, it's exactly what the council's been denying." Priya took the phone, tilted the screen against the window light, and frowned at it the way she frowned at anything that arrived uninvited.

"That's not the Willow Street underpass," Priya said. "The railing's wrong. But don't take my word for it." She pulled the laptop closer, opened a search page, and clicked something in the image box. Alice leaned in. "What are you doing?" "Checking where it's actually from," Priya said. "Google added search by image in 2011. You upload the picture, or paste its link, and it finds where else it shows up on the web." She dragged the photo from Alice's phone into the box and hit enter, and for a moment they both watched the little spinning wheel like it was a coin in the air.

The results loaded in a grid. The same flooded underpass, the same man on the roof, the same sign, on pages in Portuguese, in Turkish, in what looked like Polish. The dates marched backward: 2019, 2017, 2016. One page, a regional news site, ran it with a caption about floods in a city Alice had never heard of, in a country an ocean away. She sat back on her heels. The photo wasn't from last month, or last year, or this continent, and the sign, when she zoomed until the pixels smeared, didn't even say what the English version in her grandmother's thread said. Someone had translated the despair.

"So my grandma got played," Alice said slowly. "Somebody took an old photo and dressed it up for our town." She was aware of two feelings shoving at each other, one of them a hot loyalty to her grandmother's outrage, which was, after all, aimed at a real problem, and the other a cold dislike of being used. Priya was already screenshotting the results. "Send her this. She'd rather know now than get lambasted at the meeting when somebody stands up and fact-checks her in front of everyone." Alice typed and deleted three drafts, because each one sounded like she was correcting a child.

The family thread kept pinging. Her aunt had added the photo to a community group, four hundred members, with the caption "OUR TOWN, LAST MONTH." Someone had already written "Sharing this everywhere." Alice looked at the clock above Priya's stove: 5:40. If she said nothing, the false photo would do the rounds and then, when it collapsed, it would take a little of the real flooding complaints down with it, and people would say the whole thing was manufactured, which it partly was, in the worst way. If she spoke up, she would be the granddaughter who embarrassed her grandmother in front of the aunts. Provenance, Priya called it, tracing where a thing came from, as if every image carried a birth certificate. It apparently didn't, unless you went looking.

Alice called instead of texting. Her grandmother answered on the second ring, her voice already at rally pitch, saying she had seventeen people confirmed for the meeting and did Alice have the flyers. "Grandma, the photo isn't ours," Alice said. "It's from floods overseas, years ago. I can show you exactly where it appeared. The underpass flooding here is still real, and we can still be angry about that, but this particular picture is a costume." There was a long silence on the line, long enough that she could hear the television behind him, some moribund game show grinding through its applause.

"Send me the other pages," her grandmother finally said. "The ones with the dates." Then, quieter, almost to herself: "The man on the roof looked so much like Raymond from church." Alice promised to send everything, the links, the grid of results, the zoomed sign, and hung up to find Priya holding her phone, thumb hovering over the aunt's post in the community group. "Do we correct it publicly or let her figure it out?" Priya asked. Outside, the actual sky was going gray over the actual street, and somewhere in the flooded underpass of the internet, the man on the roof held his sign in a language neither of them could read. Alice put out her hand for the phone. "Post the links," she said. "All of them. Then we go."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
story:
The trouble began, as most troubles at Camp Wenonah did, with a clipboard. Hailey had been promoted to junior instructor two days into the second session, which meant she now carried a clipboard and had to adjudicate disputes over paddles, which felt absurd given that she could not yet reliably dock a canoe without sounding like a dropped piano. Her one official duty was to coach her fellow counselor-in-training, Priya, on the stern stroke, and to do it kindly, because Priya had asked, in her flat, terrifying way, "Tell me what I'm doing wrong. Actually tell me. Don't be nice about it."

Hailey, being eighteen and fluent in nice, had prepared carefully. She watched Priya paddle, then delivered her verdict on the dock at sunset, mosquitoes performing their interminable evening service around their heads. She praised the catch, the posture, the recovery, the timing, the way Priya didn't panic when the canoe wobbled, five separate compliments, each sincere. Then she said, "One thing: on the draw, you're dropping your wrist, so the blade slips." Priya nodded, paddled back out, and came in ten minutes later with the stroke fixed and a face like a locked door.

"Was it that bad?" Hailey asked.

"I don't remember any of the good stuff," Priya said. "Just the wrist. It's rattling around in there like a marble."

That night, in the staff tent, Hailey found a photocopied page wedged in her bunk, left over from a psych elective she'd almost taken senior year. It was a review from 2001, led by Roy Baumeister, called "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," and the first line said that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size. She read it three times by flashlight. So her five compliments and her one criticism had not been five to one at all. They had been one to one, maybe one to five, the wrist dropping through the floor of Priya's brain while the praise evaporated overhead. It wasn't a matter of causality she could blame herself for, some flaw in her delivery. It was just the arithmetic of people. She turned this over, and something in it bothered her, a whisper that said: fine, but you still chose to end on the bad part, like leaving a single sock on an otherwise clean floor.

Priya, meanwhile, was on the dock at dawn, practicing the draw stroke alone, wrist locked perfectly, and hating it. The marble had grown teeth. It occurred to her that she had asked for honesty and then punished the honesty when it arrived, which was a rotten move, and also that she could not seem to stop doing it. Every pass of the blade, she heard drop. She'd heard her mother's version of this for years, the compliment sandwich with an undisclosed center. She'd rather have the sandwich assembled in front of her, honestly, than be handed one and find the filling by surprise.

At breakfast Hailey slid her tray opposite Priya's and put the photocopy on the table. "Read the first line."

Priya read. " 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good,' " she said. "Cheerful title."

"That's what happened yesterday. I stacked five good things and one wrist, and the wrist won. It usually does." Hailey tapped the page. "So I've been thinking about how to do this differently, and I want to try again, but the rule is we build the feedback together. You tell me what kind lands."

They tried it that afternoon. Hailey watched the draw stroke, waited until Priya was mid-rhythm and not braced for judgment, and said, "Your top hand is stacking beautifully. Now, while it's still beautiful, drop the wrist on purpose so you can feel the difference, then bring it back." Priya did it, clumsy then clean, and laughed at herself, and Hailey said, "See, the blade slips when the wrist drops, but you already felt that, so I don't have to be the voice in your head saying it forever."

"You're demoting yourself from marble to footnote," Priya said, drawing the blade through green water. "I accept."

By Thursday, Priya's stroke was the best in the unit, and she'd begun coaching a twelve-year-old named Beans, who had arms like noodles and total confidence. "Your catch is strong," Priya told him. "Now let's make it strong on the left side too, and I'll do it with you." Hailey watched from the dock, clipboard against her hip, feeling that she'd worked out something true and also something incomplete, that kindness and specificity were not the same thing, and she wasn't sure yet which one did the heavy lifting.

"Hey," Priya called across the water, "Beans says my wrist thing is fixed. Tell her, Beans."

"Her wrist is a masterpiece," Beans announced, and paddled directly into the dock.

story:
Emily had the living room to herself until six, which gave her four hours, and she spent the first forty minutes of them not writing. The assignment was on the whiteboard in her mind exactly as Professor Ansel had written it: a ten-minute play drawn from a moment in your own life, staged with at least one other person. The moment she kept circling was Thanksgiving two years ago, when her brother Cal, nineteen days out of the program, had sat at the kids' table because he'd asked to, and their mother had let him, and Emily had carried both plates over and pretended it was nothing.

She opened her laptop and typed a scene between a brother and sister at a folding table. Then she deleted it, because it was Cal, unmistakably Cal, down to the way he flattened his napkin into quarters before touching the food. You couldn't just take somebody and pour him onto a stage. Their mother still cried at the smell of certain cough medicines. If Cal ever sat in an audience and heard his own sentences coming out of a stranger's mouth, what would that do to the ninety days he had now, the hundred and ten, whatever careful number he was carrying?

Her phone buzzed against the arm of the couch. A message from Priya, from the playwriting seminar: "you still stuck? thought of you today. we were talking about The Glass Menagerie in my drama lit class. Tennessee Williams based Laura, the fragile sister, on his own sister Rose. whole play is full of real her. anyway. what's your play about."

Emily read it three times. Then she looked it up herself, because Priya got things backwards sometimes, and it was true, it was in the biography she found, it was everywhere once she went looking. He had done the exact thing she was afraid of. He had taken a real sister, fragile and specific, and set her loose in a play that strangers would perform in Ohio, in London, for a hundred years probably. Emily sat with that for a while, feeling her heart palpitate in the way it did before a competition or a confession. There was something almost obstreperous about it, the way the play refused to apologize, though the play itself was quiet. Maybe the audacity and the tenderness were the same gesture. She didn't know yet. She knew only that somebody had done it and the somebody was Tennessee Williams, and that Rose had a glass menagerie now, forever, whether or not she would have chosen one.

She typed back: "my brother. thanksgiving after rehab. I keep writing him and then chickening out because it's actually him." Priya answered with a row of exclamation points and then: "williams didn't write a documentary though. laura isn't rose with the serial numbers filed off. she's laura. unicorn and everything. make yours somebody new."

Emily reread her deleted scene, which was still in the trash folder, recoverable, the way nothing in a family ever really got thrown out. The brother in it was Cal in his posture, but he wasn't Cal in his mouth. Cal would never have said the thing she'd written about being grateful for small tables. She had given that line to the brother because she needed somebody to say it, and he had said it for her, obediently, the way he'd always done what the family needed. She recovered the file.

By five o'clock she had a draft, and by five twenty she had texted Marcus, who lived two streets over and owed her for driving him to the oral surgeon. He arrived at five forty with his backpack still on, ate half the bowl of pretzels she'd set out, and asked where she wanted him. "The couch is the living room," Emily said. "The coffee table is the folding table. You're the brother, Denny. I'm the sister, but she's called Nan, and she's not me exactly, she's pushier than me."

Marcus read Denny straight through once, flatly, the way people read anything for the first time, and the words sounded thin. He looked up. "This is your family, isn't it," he said. Not a question, or not only one. Emily's face went warm. "It's based on," she started, and then decided against the veneer of that word. "It's him. Some of it. Denny's kinder than my brother is right now. That part I made up." Marcus nodded slowly and picked the script back up.

"Then let's do it like it matters," he said. He stood, moved the pretzels aside, sat down at the coffee table, and flattened an invisible napkin into quarters, which was not in the stage directions, which he could not have known was Cal's gesture, and Emily stood very still in the doorway of the kitchen with her heart going hard. Nan's first line was "You picked the kids' table on purpose," and she hadn't decided until this second whether Nan says it cruelly or gently, and the choice was going to reveal something about Emily that she hadn't admitted to anybody, herself included.

She took a breath and stepped toward the coffee table. "Six o'clock," she said, checking the clock over the mantel, because their mother would be home soon and could hear the whole thing or none of it, and Emily had not yet decided which. "From the top. And Marcus, when you say the line about the small table, don't be noble about it. Be embarrassed."

Marcus set the invisible napkin down. "Okay," he said. "From the top."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
story:
The paper came back on a Thursday, and Jeremy read it standing at his locker before he even made it to the bus. At the top, in Mr. Okonkwo's cramped green ink, sat a single sentence: "Wrong system. See me." Below it, circled twice, was his first footnote. He had spent a weekend on those footnotes. He had numbered them, formatted them, alphabetized the bibliography the way a website had shown him, and now the whole apparatus looked like a fence around an empty lot.

At the kitchen table that evening he spread the pages out between his mother's mail and a bowl of untouched grapes. His little sister, Dara, leaned over his shoulder long enough to steal a grape and ask what a superscript was. "A tiny number that means I did work," he said, and she said, "It looks like the work did you." He flicked a grape stem at her and she left, taking the bowl.

He opened his laptop beside the ruined paper and typed the assignment sheet's phrase into the search bar: Chicago style. What came back surprised him. Chicago style offered two citation systems, the screen said. There was notes and bibliography, which people used in history and the humanities, and there was author-date, common in the sciences. He sat back. He had not known there were two. He had copied whichever example the first website had shown him, which turned out to be author-date, a name-and-year in parentheses, the kind of thing his chemistry lab reports used. He had built his history paper, footnotes and all, on the science system.

"That's like putting the wrong engine in a car," his mother said when she came in with groceries. She set a bag of oranges on the counter. "Everything runs, technically."

"It doesn't run. He wrote 'see me' like I committed a crime."

"Then go see him." She rolled an orange across the table to him. "Eat something. You look like a footnote yourself."

At school the next morning he did see him, briefly, before the bell. Mr. Okonkwo did not lecture. He tapped the circled footnote with one finger and said, "Notes and bibliography for my class, Jeremy. Author-date is for the sciences." Then he handed back Jeremy's thesis paragraph, which had no mark on it at all, and said, "The argument's not the problem." That was all, and somehow it invigorated Jeremy more than any speech would have, because it meant the ideas had survived and only the plumbing was wrong.

That weekend the table became a workshop. He learned that in notes and bibliography the first note gave the full citation and the second gave a shortened one, which struck him as almost courteous, a formal introduction followed by a nod. He learned that the bibliography ignored "A" and "The" when alphabetizing, a rule so petty he laughed out loud at the kitchen table, alone, at ten at night. Dara wandered down for water and found him with fourteen tabs open. "What's the paper about?" she asked, and he told her: whether the city's decision to close the neighborhood pools had been about money or about who swam where, and his answer was that it was both, and that the two motives were tangled in a way the archives didn't cleanly separate. "So you don't know," Dara said.

"I know part of it. The rest I have to say I don't know, and show why."

"That's a weird thing to hand in." She filled her glass and went back upstairs, and he kept working.

On Monday he printed the new draft and reread it at the table before school. The footnotes sat in their proper system now, full then shortened, the bibliography at the end in its own order. But rereading his conclusion, he found a sentence he'd written at two in the morning, something trenchant about the pool commission hiding its motives, and he could no longer find a note that supported it. It sounded strong. It sounded exactly like the kind of thing that had no evidence behind it. He sat with his pen over the page for a long minute while the toaster popped up behind him, unattended.

He crossed the sentence out. In its place he wrote a smaller, more careful claim, and added a footnote to a budget memo he had actually read, and after the citation, in the note itself, he typed: "The commission's private correspondence remains sealed; this remains uncertain." It felt like a strange thing to hand in, an admission riding along at the bottom of the page like a passenger. He stapled the pages, slid them into his backpack, and reached over and took the last orange.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
story:
Mathis arrived at the track at six-forty with a cone bag, a clipboard, and the private suspicion that coaching was mostly standing around while other people made mistakes. He had been given the under-fourteens because nobody else wanted them, and their weakness was specific enough to be embarrassing: they could not pass over any distance longer than ten meters without the ball wobbling sideways like something drunk. He had watched them lose twice. Both times the passes went wrong in the same way, and both times their previous coach, Mr. Audet, had shouted a correction after every single attempt, so that by the final whistle the boys looked like puppets waiting for the next tug on the string.

He had found the answer, or something like an answer, at one in the morning, in a psychology textbook his sister had left on the kitchen table. There was a term for it in the research on how people learn movement. He read the page three times, then copied two sentences into his phone so he would not soften them later. In the morning the sentences still said the same thing, which he took as a good sign.

"Okay," he said, setting the cones in pairs twenty meters apart. "We're doing the passing drill. But here's the deal. I'm only going to say something after every fifth pass. Not every one. Not every one."

"That's it?" said Ilyes, who was twelve and already suspicious of adults bearing plans.

"That's it."

The first twenty minutes were, from a coaching standpoint, close to unwatchable. Passes skipped off ankles, rose into the turbid gray of the morning sky, and once traveled a full ninety degrees from where anyone was standing. Mathis bit down on the urge to speak. His whole body felt like a held note. When the fifth pass came, a good one, he said only, "That. Do that again," and then went quiet, and the boys looked at him as if he had short-changed them.

Afterward Ilyes cornered him by the equipment shed. The subtext of the conversation was not hard to read, though neither of them named it: the kid wanted to know whether he was being neglected or trained, and he wanted Mathis to say which, and Mathis understood that whatever he answered would be remembered longer than any drill. "You're not ignoring us because you don't care?" Ilyes said, which was a question shaped like an accusation.

"It's called the guidance hypothesis," Mathis said. "Feedback after every single attempt can make you dependent on it. Less frequent feedback helps retention. So I'm not ignoring you. I'm rationing myself." He heard how it sounded, like a boy quoting a textbook on a track, and he did not entirely mind, because it was also true, and Ilyes seemed to prefer an argument to a reassurance.

That night he wrote to Mr. Audet, because the man had asked, twice, to be kept informed, and because some part of Mathis wanted a witness in case the whole thing collapsed. "Dear Mr. Audet," the letter began, and he kept it short. "The boys' passing was poor over distance, so I built a drill, twenty-meter pairs, fifth-pass feedback only. They complain that I say nothing. Their completion rate on the long ball went from maybe half to eight out of ten by Thursday, but I can't tell yet whether that's the drill or the weather or them deciding I'm not worth arguing with. I know you corrected every pass when you had them. I'm not trying to say you were wrong. I'm trying the other thing. If they fall apart in the match, I'll accept that, but I'd like you to see it either way. Mathis." He read it over, decided it did not absolve him of anything, which felt correct, and sent it.

On Saturday the under-fourteens played a team in yellow shirts who were bigger and slower. For ten minutes nothing happened. Then Ilyes took the ball at the halfway line, and there was a stretch of silence where the whole sideline seemed to lean, and he struck a flat twenty-five-meter pass that arrived at Kylian's feet like a delivered letter. Kylian scored. Mathis, standing on the touchline with his arms crossed, said absolutely nothing, and caught Ilyes glancing over at him afterward anyway, checking, and then looking away, and then doing it again. Mr. Audet was there in a green coat near the corner flag, watching Mathis more than the game, holding whatever he thought in his mouth like a coin. The score was one-one with six minutes left. Ilyes had the ball again, thirty meters out, and no one to pass to except everyone.
