activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
story:
The router at Grand-mère's house reached only as far as the kitchen, so Antoine carried his laptop into the study, where his grandfather's books still held the shelves like an occupying army. The assignment was due in eleven days: a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. He had a paragraph on Burke and a paragraph on conservative historians who saw the whole thing as a descent into chaos, and then nothing, a blank that had begun to feel personal.

"You're not going to sit in there all afternoon," his grandmother said from the doorway, querulous in the way of someone who has already decided the answer. "Those books need sorting. Your grandfather kept everything, and I am not leaving that job to your uncle." She wanted the study emptied by September, that was the real project, and Antoine suspected his essay had arrived as a convenient instrument of it.

He agreed to sort, which meant pulling books off shelves and stacking them into piles marked, in his grandmother's hand, Garder, Donner, Jeter. Most of them were agronomy journals and railway timetables from the sixties. Then, wedged flat behind a row of almanacs, he found four fat volumes in red cloth: Histoire socialiste de la Révolution française, by Jean Jaurès. Socialist, in the title itself, like a flavor announcement.

He recognized the name, but not from the title page. He'd seen it that morning on the war memorial in the village square, where he'd gone to escape the kitchen. Among the names of the dead of 1914 there was a separate plaque, and on it, alone, Jaurès, assassinated in 1914. A single man with his own plaque, not among the soldiers. Antoine had stood there eating a stale croissant and wondering who rated that.

Now he sat on the floor with volume one open on his knees. His grandfather had underlined in soft pencil, never pen, the way a connoisseur of margins might, and in the front cover there was a bookseller's stamp from a shop on a street that no longer appeared on maps. The copyright pages put the writing in the early 1900s. Jaurès, then, was a historian, and also dead on a plaque, and the introduction, dense and self-assured, argued that the Revolution should be read as the rising of a class against another class, the bourgeoisie against the old order, and the people beneath both, fermenting.

Antoine's essay had no section like that. He had the noble version and the horror version and nothing between, which, he now understood, was like writing about weather without mentioning summer.

He carried volume two to the kitchen, where his grandmother was boiling something she would later insist was simple. "Do you know anything about Jaurès?" he asked.

"He was a socialist politician," she said, tapping the spoon. "They killed him just before the war. Your grandfather worshipped him. He said every history teacher after that man taught the Revolution as classes fighting classes, right up to when he retired." She tasted the pot. "He thought it was lazy. He also thought it was true."

Antoine went back and wrote for two hours, sorting books only when he heard her footsteps on the stairs. His paragraph on Burke now had a companion: the class-conflict reading, born of one assassinated deputy's four volumes, dominant for most of the century, his grandfather's whole career conducted inside its shadow. He drafted a sentence about how a history written to serve a political hope could still organize a hundred years of teaching, then deleted the word "still," because he wasn't sure the caveat was honest.

The uncertainty he could not draft his way past was simpler. He didn't know whether the historians who came after Jaurès had refined the class interpretation or merely inherited it, and his grandfather's penciled margins offered opinions, not evidence. The internet remained in the kitchen, the kitchen contained his grandmother, and his grandmother contained plans for the Garder pile that did not include four red volumes.

At dinner he laid out the problem in the flattest terms available: noble Revolution, terrible Revolution, class war, and himself, undecided between them, with eleven days minus one remaining.

"That is not a problem," his grandmother said, cutting her bread. "That is an essay. You put the three of them in a room and you say what they cannot agree on." She pointed her knife at him. "And the Jaurès stays in the Garder pile. That one is not for the university. That one is mine."

Afterward he found her in the study, volume two open on the desk where his grandfather must have read it, her finger moving slowly under a line of print he had not marked.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
story:
The substitute had left a worksheet on the front table with a note that read "Due by end of period," and Kyle read it twice before touching his stool. Behind him, the incubator hummed, and someone's forgotten beaker of bromothymol blue sat by the sink, its color gone faintly yellow. He had missed Tuesday for a dentist appointment, which meant he had missed the lecture on cellular respiration, and now the worksheet wanted him to trace glucose all the way to ATP in the mitochondria, arrow by arrow, with the exam on Friday looming behind it like weather.

He started with what he knew. Glucose got split, that much he remembered from middle school, and somewhere at the end the cell got ATP, its spendable energy. Between those two points the worksheet expected a chain of boxes: glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, something called the electron transport chain. He filled in the first two from the textbook's diagrams, then stopped at a sentence in the margins about a gradient and felt his pencil hover. Around him the room smelled of dish soap and the ghost of yesterday's yeast lab, and the clock over the door gave him fifty minutes.

Dana leaned over from the next station, her own sheet already flipped to the back. "You look like the worksheet insulted your family."

"It kind of did." He tapped the empty box. "It says the electrons pass down the chain and then, quote, a gradient drives ATP synthesis. Drives it how? A gradient isn't a thing you can push with."

She pulled her sheet back and chewed her pen cap, thinking. On her family's farm in the valley there was a pond above an old earthen dam, and every spring the snowmelt backed up behind it until the water stood high and heavy, waiting. "The protons pile up on one side," she said slowly. "Like water behind a dam. They want to go back through, and when they do, the cell makes ATP."

Kyle looked at her, then at the diagram. So the chain wasn't the whole story; it was a pump, spending electrons to stack protons on one side of a membrane, storing pressure the way the pond stored snowmelt. The word gradient stopped being a vocabulary term and became something you could almost hear, a straining quietness, like the pond before the spillway gate opened. He wrote protons build up on one side of the membrane and flow back through, driving ATP synthesis, and the sentence felt less like copying than like arriving somewhere.

"The book says a guy named Peter Mitchell proposed this in 1961," Dana said, reading off her page. "Won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. There's a name for it, too. Chemiosmosis." She pronounced it carefully, once, like a word she was testing for cracks.

Kyle had been ready to impugn the whole unit an hour ago, to file the worksheet away as another indictment of a curriculum that demanded names before it gave anyone a picture. Now the names felt earned. Mitchell had looked at a membrane and seen a dam, which sounded grandiose until you tried it yourself and found it was the only image that held. Still, Kyle's diagram had a gap he couldn't close: he had drawn the protons flowing back through, but the textbook's arrow pointed the opposite direction on one page, and he could not tell whether the book was wrong or he was. He copied both versions into the margin, side by side, honest about which one he trusted and which one he didn't yet.

The substitute drifted past, checked the clock, and said, "Ten minutes, folks." Dana was already sealing her sheet. Kyle spent nine of the ten minutes drawing the dam in the margin of his own paper: the pond dark and full, the gate at the bottom, a small wheel turning where the water left. He labeled nothing on it. On the actual worksheet he wrote his answer with the two contradictory arrows still visible beneath, then signed his name.

At the sink he rinsed the yellowed beaker and watched the color run out of it, thinning toward clear. Dana shouldered her bag on her way to the door. "Friday," she said. "Bring the dam."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
story:
Rose had come to the museum to escape the physics exam she would fail on Monday, which was a contradiction she intended not to examine too closely. The ballistics exhibit on the second floor was nearly empty, a long hall where a pneumatic launcher fired small brass spheres at different angles into a net, and a placard beside it asked visitors to predict where each ball would land.

She stood at the console and typed her guess into the keypad: angle forty-five degrees, speed twelve meters per second, so the marker slid along the rail to a point on the floor. The ball arced, dropped, and hit the floor a full meter short of her marker. She had used a formula from the back of her textbook, copied it letter for letter, and it had lied to her, or she had lied to herself with its help.

A boy in a museum volunteer shirt was stacking spare spheres in a cart. He was taciturn in the way of people who had decided most questions weren't worth the breath, and when she asked him whether the machine was calibrated wrong, he only said, "It's not the machine," and kept stacking.

Rose stayed anyway. Her mother had wanted her to go into the deposition office on Saturday and sign the papers for the insurance claim, the formal statement about the car accident in April, the one where the facts had to be given once and then never revised. She had promised to go after the museum. It was that errand, more than the exam, that had her jaw set tight.

In April, in the hospital, her mother had said, "It's physics, Rose, it's nobody's fault, ice on the road." That was supposed to allay something, Rose supposed, the guilt or the anger, and it had worked on neither. What she remembered instead was the ambulance ceiling sliding past, and thinking with strange clarity that the car had flown, briefly, that there had been an arc.

She typed another guess at the console and missed again. Then a girl about ten years old, dragging a bored father, punched in a wild prediction and got closer than Rose had. The girl had simply watched the previous ball and put her finger where it landed, a method Rose couldn't argue with.

So Rose watched too. She asked for the angle to be set to sixty degrees and the speed to twelve, and she counted under her breath, one one-thousand, two one-thousand, while the ball rose, hung, fell. The ball left the launcher at twelve meters per second, she knew that much, and at sixty degrees most of that speed was pointed upward, about ten and a half of it. She remembered, from somewhere in the back of the textbook, that gravity pulled the vertical speed down at 9.8 meters per second every second. So the ball should reach the top of its arc a little over one second after launch. She counted to the top and got about one second, and then she counted the fall, and it took about one second more.

The whole flight was twice the rise. That was the thing she had missed. She had found the time to the top of the arc in her homework on Friday and written it down as the total time, and Mr. Okafor had marked it with a red slash, no correction offered, the class out of time. Rising and falling take equal times, she said to herself, and because there was no one to say it to, she said it to the volunteer. "The time up equals the time down."

He looked at the net, then at her, and gave her the shortest nod she had ever received, which somehow felt like a prize.

She worked it through with the keypad. Total flight time, twice the vertical part of the speed divided by gravity: two times 10.5 divided by 9.8, call it 2.1 seconds. The horizontal part of the speed at sixty degrees was only about 6 meters per second, constant the whole way, so the ball should land around 13 meters out. She moved the marker, fired, and the brass sphere rang into the net six inches from her guess.

She did it again at thirty degrees, then at forty-five, and each time the marker sat where the ball fell, and each time the numbers she wrote in her notebook agreed with the floor. The two directions were separate, that was the whole trick; you let the vertical part slow and reverse while the horizontal part just went, and they met again at the landing.

The volunteer, restocking the launcher, said without looking at her, "You're the first person today to use the keypad twice."

"It took me a while," Rose said. "I made the same mistake at school. Found the time to the top and forgot to double it for the whole flight."

He shrugged, almost warmly.

Her phone buzzed in her pocket. Her mother, asking if she was on her way to the deposition office, reminding her that they wanted the statement today, one version, final, no second pass the way there was no second pass for a car leaving the road. Rose looked at the keypad, at the brass spheres gleaming in their rack, at the long bright arc she could now predict on paper but could not, in April, have done anything about.

She closed her notebook, put it in her bag, and typed one more angle into the console before she left: sixty degrees, speed twelve, marker set, ball away. It rose, hung, fell, and landed where she said it would, and she turned and walked toward the stairs.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
story:
The community centre on Delmore Street smelled of floor wax and instant coffee, and on Thursday evenings the music room belonged to whoever signed the sheet on the door. Joseph had signed it for six weeks now, mostly to have somewhere that was not his house, and mostly because the piano there was only slightly out of tune.

He sat at the table by the window with his staff paper, trying to fit a melody into sixteen bars. The melody itself had come easily, humming out of him on the bus, something in a minor key that his younger sister had called melancholic when he played it for her, though she had said it kindly, the way she noticed things about him he didn't say out loud. The trouble was the chords. He knew they existed. He knew they belonged with the melody somehow, the way a voice belongs with the words it carries. Beyond that, everything was fog.

"I want to play it with you," said Priya, dropping into the chair across from him with her coat still on. She had heard him through the door the week before and had come to find out what it was. "Not the melody. I'd take the accompaniment. If you ever finish it."

"It's finished," Joseph said, turning the paper toward her. "It's the rest of it that isn't."

Priya looked at the staff, at the notes marching across five lines and four spaces, and then at the empty space above them. "So write the chords there," she said. "Above the staff. C, Am, G7, whatever they are. On a lead sheet, the chord symbols go above the staff so I know which chord goes with each part of the melody."

Joseph looked at the empty ceiling of his own page as though it had been waiting for him to notice it. "That's how it works?"

"That's how it works for every pianist who's ever sight-read anything. You give me the melody and the symbols, I do the rest." She pulled the pencil from behind her ear and slid it back to him. "But they have to be the right ones."

That was the part that kept him there past eight o'clock. He tried a C under the opening phrase because the phrase started on C and that felt like obedience, but when Priya played it, the chord sat under the melody like a stone under a leaf. He tried Am instead, and the whole bar went dark in a way he recognized, the way his melody had sounded in his head on the bus before he'd tried to make it polite. He had been thinking of the two tasks as separate, melody one thing and harmony another, when really they were more like consanguinity, a family resemblance between notes, the same blood in different faces. Some chords were cousins to his tune and some were strangers wearing its coat.

He worked bar by bar, writing a symbol, listening to Priya's hands, crossing it out when it lied. Where his melody climbed toward something hopeful, he wanted a chord that climbed with it, and where it sank back into itself he wanted one that sank too, and these two wants argued in him the whole evening. Neatness, his father's voice in his head, the belief that a thing should resolve, should end where a listener can rest. And underneath that, his sister's word, melancholic, the suspicion that the tune was true exactly because it didn't want to be comforted. He didn't know yet which of them he acceded to, and he decided, somewhere in bar eleven, that he was allowed not to know, that he could let the chords disagree with each other the way he did.

"You've got two bars left," Priya said. Her tea had gone cold beside her; she'd been playing for over an hour without mentioning it, and he noticed that now, the way she kept her hands ready over the keys whenever he looked up, waiting for him. "The end. Where does it land?"

He studied the last phrase. It circled and didn't settle, and every chord he considered felt like a decision about something larger than the four beats in front of him. He wrote G7 above the fifteenth bar, held the pencil over the sixteenth, and let it hover.

"Play that," he said.

She played it, the G7 pulling the phrase forward into the empty final bar, into the question he hadn't answered. Then she lifted her hands and looked at him across the piano.

"Well?" she said. "Am or C?"

Joseph tapped the pencil twice against the edge of the table, then leaned down and wrote something small above the last bar.

"Both," he said. "Let's hear it."

story:
Julia spread the two leases across the kitchen table like cards she intended to win with, though she had never played a hand of anything in her life. The first came from Mrs. Okafor's basement unit on King Street, fourteen hundred a month, heat and water included, hydro extra. The second came from a man named Terek, third floor of a house near campus, twelve fifty, and under the heading Utilities a line that just said "tenant responsible," which could mean anything from forty dollars to a number with three digits.

She had told Devi, over the phone the night before, that she was basically an expert at this now. That wasn't quite true. What was true was that she had read both documents twice and made a spreadsheet, and that she wanted very badly to be the kind of person who handled things, the kind who did not need her mother hovering behind her asking whether she had checked the water heater. Her mother was at work. The house was quiet except for the fridge.

"Twelve fifty plus utilities," Devi had said. "Call the hydro company. Ask what the last tenant paid."

"Landlords have to tell you that," Julia had said, with more confidence than the claim deserved. She was still getting used to how easily certainty arrived when someone needed it from her.

The numbers came first, because numbers were the part she trusted. She opened the spreadsheet and typed the rent, then added an estimate for hydro at the King Street unit, seventy a month, since only lights and outlets were hers there. For Terek's place the line stayed blank. The blank bothered her more than a bad number would have. A bad number was at least a fact she could argue with.

Then she noticed the documents themselves, which she had been treating as containers for numbers rather than as things with their own logic. Mrs. Okafor's lease ran fourteen pages, dense, bureaucratic, with a phrase at the top she recognized from a government website she had visited at two in the morning: Residential Tenancy Agreement, Standard Form of Lease. Terek's was four pages. His looked tidy, businesslike, and slightly obdurate about it, like a man who had decided long ago how his properties would be run and had printed that decision on letter paper. He had written in his own rules about guests and cleaning, and there was a clause about a "final cleaning disbursement" of two hundred dollars due on the first of the month, every month, which Julia read three times before she understood it was not a deposit but a fee that would underpin his income no matter what condition she kept the place in.

She called Devi back. "One of them uses the government standard lease form and one doesn't. The Okafor one. The Terek one is just, like, his own document."

"Is that allowed?"

"I don't think so. For Ontario. I read that most private residential landlords have to use the government's standard lease form for new leases. And if they don't give you one, you can ask for it in writing."

"So write to him."

"I haven't decided anything yet."

"You made a spreadsheet, Julia. You've decided."

She hadn't, though, and the reason she hadn't was the reason she hadn't told Devi about the cleaning fee yet. Twelve fifty plus two hundred was fourteen fifty before utilities, which meant the cheaper apartment was probably not cheaper, and Julia had spent four days telling herself she loved the third floor and its slanted ceilings and its distance from her mother's kitchen. She had told her mother it was about independence. She had told herself that too. Whether it had ever been true, she could no longer say; the wanting had hardened into a position, and positions are difficult to examine from inside.

She wrote the email anyway, because writing it cost nothing and because some part of her wanted to see what Terek would do. "I'm interested in the unit," she typed, "and before signing I'd like to request, in writing, that you provide me with the government standard form of lease." She read it over, deleted "I'd like to" and put in "I am requesting," and sent it before she could soften it further. Then she sat at the table with both leases in front of her and the fridge humming, and she remembered being twelve, standing in a school hallway, telling a teacher her project was done when it was in her backpack half-finished, and how the teacher had believed her, and how that had felt like a power and then, walking home, like a debt.

Terek replied within the hour. The email was two lines. The first said the standard form would be provided to the successful applicant. The second said that, due to the number of inquiries, the monthly cleaning disbursement would be increasing to two hundred and fifty effective September.

Julia laughed once, out loud, alone in the kitchen, a short sound with no warmth in it. Then she picked up her phone and photographed the email, and photographed both leases, and typed the new number into her spreadsheet, and watched the total climb past Mrs. Okafor's fourteen hundred by a margin that no amount of slanted ceiling could justify. She stared at the two totals for a long moment. Then she scrolled to her mother's contact and pressed call, and while it rang she squared the pages on the table so their edges lined up exactly.

"Mom," she said. "Do you still have Mrs. Okafor's number?"

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
Alicia had told herself, all summer, that she didn't care about the market stall anymore, that handing it over to Priya had been a practical decision and not a retreat, and by September she almost believed it. Then Ms. Okonkwo set a block of couverture on each station and said only, "Today we temper. You'll know it worked when it snaps." The marble slab was cold under Alicia's palms. She melted the chocolate to forty-five degrees, poured two thirds onto the slab, and worked it with a palette knife, spreading and scraping, spreading and scraping, watching the glossy ribbon turn matte at its edges. Priya, one station over, moved her knife in the same rhythm, and neither of them spoke, which was its own kind of sentence.

The trick, according to the worksheet, was seeding: a handful of chopped chocolate stirred into the warm mass to coax the right crystals into forming. Too warm and they dissolved, too cool and the wrong ones took over, leaving chocolate that bent instead of snapping and bloomed with gray streaks by morning. Alicia found herself thinking in two registers at once. There was the chemistry teacher's way of talking about it, all crystal forms and stable lattices, and there was her grandmother's way, which had been nothing but a firm wrist and the flat statement that chocolate knows when you are impatient. She had always dichotomized those approaches, science versus feel, as though a person had to pick a tribe. Working the slab, she wasn't sure the line was anywhere real. The thermometer told her when to stop; the sheen under the fluorescent lights told her too, a half-second sooner.

She tested it the way the worksheet said: she touched a smear to her lip. It should feel cool, slightly cooler than skin, and it did, and she dipped a square of parchment and set it in the fridge's chill. When she broke it, the crack was audible across the room, clean as a knuckle popping. Ms. Okonkwo looked over and gave a single nod, which from her was not litotes but a full ovation.

What Alicia didn't say, that afternoon, was that she had tried this once before. In her memory she had quit the stall because of exams, and because her mother was ill that spring, and both things were true, and also there had been a Saturday in April when the chocolate bloomed gray in the sun and a customer asked for her money back and Alicia stood there feeling twelve years old, and she had not gone back the following week. Priya had gone instead, with a borrowed table and a borrowed confidence. Alicia was telling herself the story of the practical decision right up until Priya slid her own test square across the aisle and said, "Yours snapped louder," and grinned, and something in Alicia's chest rearranged itself without permission.

From Priya's side of the aisle, it looked different, and fairness demanded that version too. Priya had watched her friend abandon the stall the way you watch someone wade out of cold water, all at once and pretending it was nothing, and Priya had kept the stall alive through nothing more glamorous than waking up early. She had texted Alicia that night, after the class:

Tried tempering again with the stuff you left in my fridge. Third attempt actually snapped. Guess who taught herself. Guess who's morose about it though. Come to the market Saturday, we're a two person stall or we're nothing. Also I still don't get why yours worked and mine bloomed in June. Explain the science part. You're the one who reads.

Alicia read the message four times. The first reading stung, because Priya made quitting sound like a choice with a witness. The second reading noticed that Priya had not actually said that. The third and fourth were gentler, and by the last one Alicia understood she was holding a small piece of evidence that her summer-long account of herself was a draft, not a document.

Saturday was warm for October, and the fold-up tables at the market held trays of the chocolates they had tempered on Friday, dark squares with a shine like wet river stones. A woman stopped, lifted a piece, held it a long moment, and frowned at her own fingers. "It's warm out," she said. "Why hasn't this melted on the table? It's not even soft." Her husband picked one up and popped it straight into his mouth and made a small startled sound, because it was dissolving there, unmistakably, into something warm and slick.

Alicia heard herself answer before she decided to. "Form V cocoa butter crystals," she said. "They melt at about thirty-three point eight degrees Celsius, just below body temperature. That's why well-tempered chocolate melts in the mouth but not in the hand." Priya, wrapping the woman's purchase, mouthed the words along with her, half a beat behind, like a cue she'd been waiting for all morning. Whether the grandmother's wrist or the worksheet had carried her to this table, Alicia still couldn't say, and she watched the couple walk off eating with their eyes closed, and she reached for the next tray.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
story:
The assignment was due Monday, and Nolan had chosen it the way he chose most things, late and against a deadline. Apply one critical lens to one passage from a classic novel, his professor had written on the syllabus, and Nolan had circled it twice during his shift at Halloran's Books, the pencil leaving a gray smudge on the paper. He had until closing to pick the passage, and the stack of yellowed hardcovers his grandfather had dropped off that morning sat on the counter between him and the decision.

"Those are all going in the classics section," Mrs. Halloran said from the register, counting coins into paper rolls. "Except anything with water damage. You know how to check."

He did know. He tilted each book under the lamp, fanned the pages, and it was on the third one, a clothbound Jane Eyre with a faded spine, that he stopped. The title page read, in cramped Victorian type, Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, edited by Currer Bell. Nolan turned the page expecting another name and found none. He set the book on the counter and took out his phone, and after a minute of searching he sat back on his stool. Charlotte Brontë had first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, and nothing on the title page told a buyer that its author was a woman. He read it twice, then closed the phone and left the book open on the counter.

Priya came in at four, as she did on Thursdays, carrying a coffee and her battered Norton anthology. She was doing the same assignment and had already claimed a passage from Heart of Darkness, which she declared a pithy target for a postcolonial reading. "What did you pick?" she asked, and he slid the Brontë across the counter.

"Currer Bell," he said. "That's not her real name."

"Whose?"

"Charlotte Brontë's. This edition's from her grandfather's library or something. Look at the date."

She looked. "Huh," she said, which for Priya was a long speech, and she pulled a stool around to his side of the counter.

He had marked the passage with a receipt: the scene where Jane, governess at Thornfield, considers her position, thirty pounds a year and a room of her own, and tells herself that women feel just as men feel. He read it aloud, quietly, because a customer was browsing travel. "So which lens," Priya said. "Feminist, obviously. She's saying it out loud."

"That's what I thought first." He turned the receipt over. On the back he had written, in his cramped hand, wage, inheritance, who owns the house. "But look at the money part. She's paid thirty pounds by a man who owns everything she stands on. If you read it that way, the marriage plot is a property plot. Rochester buys her time, then wants to buy the rest of her."

Priya tapped the title page. "And this is the property plot too. The publisher buys the book, and the woman can't even sign it."

Nolan wrote that down. He wrote fast, the way he did when a sentence arrived whole, and then he sat looking at it, because something about it bothered him. "It's not the same thing, though," he said. "The pen name and the wage. One's about hiding, the other's about paying."

"So do both."

"That's not a paper, that's two papers stapled together."

She laughed, and the customer at travel gave them a look and left without buying anything. Mrs. Halloran said nothing, only looked up once and went back to her coins.

Nolan tried a draft on the back of the receipt. The governess, he wrote, becomes a synecdoche for every unmarried woman with education and no property, one figure standing for a whole class, and the class is what the novel can't stop thinking about even when it's thinking about love. Then, lower: the pseudonym reifies the condition the novel describes, turning a woman into a marketable signature, a thing with a price that changes depending on the name attached. He read both sentences back and crossed out half of the second one. It sounded borrowed, like he was wearing someone else's coat.

"I can't tell if the pen name proves the feminist reading or the Marxist one," he said. "If she'd signed it Charlotte Brontë, would the book have sold differently? I don't actually know. I can't know."

"That's the part you write down," Priya said. "The part you don't know."

"You think professors give credit for not knowing?"

"I think they give credit for noticing which questions the lens can't answer."

Closing came at six. Mrs. Halloran locked the till and told him to shelve the grandfather's books before he left, classics under the front window, spines out. He carried them in stacks of five. The Brontë went last, and before he shelved it he opened it once more to the title page, took out his phone, and photographed Currer Bell where the lamplight caught the old type. Then he slid it into its place between two other dark spines, and stood there a moment with his fingers still on the cloth cover.

"Thirty pounds a year," he said, to the window, to no one.

"I heard you," Priya called from the door, coffee cup in hand. "Put it in the first paragraph."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
story:
Sofia's uncle had given her the graph on Thursday, folded into quarters, and told her that if she could explain it to the summer kids at the quarry by Saturday, she could run the nature station on her own. The quarry was the town's unofficial swimming hole, a flooded pit with a ledge the older kids jumped from, and on Saturday mornings Sofia's aunt set up a folding table near the gravel path where the trail came down. Sofia had volunteered without quite meaning to, the way you raise your hand before you have the answer.

The graph showed carbon dioxide in the atmosphere across the last century, a line climbing in small jagged steps like a staircase someone had built without a level. Sofia understood the axes. What she could not do was say the sentence, the one that connected the line to the air over the quarry, without it coming out like a recitation. Greenhouse gases, she kept beginning, and then stalling, because she knew the phrase but not the picture.

Dana arrived first, as she always did, carrying two iced coffees and the insouciant certainty that everything would be fine, including things Dana had not studied. She set one cup in front of Sofia without being asked, having noticed that Sofia's hands were clenched around the graph's folded corners. "You've got this," Dana said. "You explained tides to me last summer and I still remember it."

"Nobody's here yet," Sofia said. "That's the problem."

While they waited, Dana pulled out her phone. She had gone to a planetarium talk on Wednesday for extra credit, and a student there had asked whether climate predictions only started with computers. Dana had looked it up on the bus home and had meant to tell Sofia, and had then, characteristically, gotten distracted. "In 1896," she read, "a Swedish scientist named Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled."

Sofia took the phone and read it again herself. No computers. No satellites. 1896, a man with pencil and paper, and somehow the same number people still argued about. It did not make the graph easier, exactly, but it made it heavier. Somebody had been watching this line before there was a line.

The kids came down the trail around ten, a loose herd of nine-year-olds and a few bored twelve-year-olds trailing behind. Sofia set the graph on the table and weighted the corners with flat quarry stones. She had planned a speech. Instead she found herself asking whether any of them had ever left a car with the windows up in a parking lot. Hands went up. "The air inside gets hot faster than the air outside," she said, "because the glass lets the sunlight in and then holds the warm air. Some gases in the sky do that to the whole Earth. Carbon dioxide is one of them. It lets sunlight in and holds the heat." That was not exactly right in every detail, and she knew it; the real mechanism was subtler than a car. She decided to be honest about that. "It's not exactly like a car," she added. "It's more like that than like nothing."

Then she showed them the line. "This is how much carbon dioxide was in the air every year, starting a hundred years ago." A boy named Marcus, one of the bored twelve-year-olds, leaned in, and his boredom seemed to undergo a small attrition, wearing away at the edges. "It never goes down," he said. "Not once."

"Not in this whole graph," Sofia said.

That night, after the station was folded up and her aunt had driven the younger kids home, Sofia wrote to her uncle, because he hated the phone and answered letters within the week. She told him about Dana's fact, the Swedish scientist and 1896 and the doubling, and how strange it was that the oldest prediction and the newest computers were describing the same Earth. She told him she still could not say whether the heat was held or slowed or bounced back; she had said "held" all afternoon and it had worked, but she suspected she had simplified it past the truth and did not know where the line was. She asked if the little jagged wiggles in the graph meant anything or were just noise, and she admitted she might be asking a question with a boring answer.

His reply came Tuesday, a single index card in a stamped envelope. "The wiggles are real. Ask me why in person." Below that he had written, "The kids will remember the staircase. They will not remember the mechanism. You gave them the staircase."

On Saturday Sofia arrived early, before Dana, and set the graph out herself, weighing the corners with the same four flat stones. Marcus came down the trail first, alone, hands in his pockets. He stopped at the table and looked at the line for a while, then put one finger on the top edge of it, where the graph ran out of years. "What happens here?" he said. "Past the edge."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
story:
Eli had been planning to say nothing, which was why Coach Reyes had commandeered the last ten minutes of practice for a captains' talk and then left the gym, making it Eli's problem. The problem was Marcus. Marcus had missed Thursday's practice and been late on Saturday, and today, in the scrimmage, he kept sagging off his man in the corner, the same corner where River Grove had hit four threes the last time they played them. Everyone knew it. Nobody said it. Dara had tried at the water break, in the tone she used on her little brother, and Marcus had gone petulant and silent for the rest of the drill, shooting free throws like each one had personally offended him.

Eli's mother was a therapist, which meant their kitchen table was full of paperbacks with dog-eared pages, and one of them, the Gottman one, had a chapter he'd read mostly by accident while eating cereal. A complaint addresses a specific behavior, the book said. Criticism attacks the person's character. His mom used the example of dishes: "you didn't rinse the pan this morning" versus "you never think about anyone but yourself." Eli had assumed it was a marriage thing, boring, until he watched Dara tell Marcus he was lazy, watched Marcus's shoulders climb toward his ears, and thought: that word, always, that's the attack part. That's the poison in it.

Not that he had any right to psychoanalyze anyone. He was sixteen and had once told his little sister she was annoying, in front of her friends, and still felt the specific burn of it two years later. But there was a difference between knowing a thing and watching it happen in front of you to someone on your own team, someone you had to pass to on Tuesday.

So after practice, when the gym had emptied to the squeak of one manager collecting balls, Eli caught Marcus by the bleachers. Marcus had his headphones half on already, one ear free, which was something, a small door left open.

"Hey," Eli said. "Can I say one thing about the scrimmage?"

Marcus pulled the headphone out all the way. "If this is about Saturday."

"It's about the corner. The guy you were guarding hit four threes in the scrimmage because you were dropping five feet off him. I counted." He kept his voice flat, like reading a stat sheet. "You missed practice Thursday and you were late Saturday, so maybe you didn't see the drill we ran on closing out. That's all it is. You weren't there for it."

Marcus stared at him. "Dara said I was lazy."

"You're not lazy. You were late twice and you were guarding the corner wrong." Eli shrugged. "Those are things that happened, not things you are."

There was a silence in which Eli became extremely interested in the floor. Then Marcus said, quietly, "My mom's shifts changed. Saturdays I have to take my sister to her lesson before I can get here. I keep meaning to tell Coach."

"That's a complaint too, I guess," Eli said. "Like, a real one. The kind you take to Coach instead of just taking the fine and saying nothing."

Marcus laughed, a short, surprised sound. "Where'd you get this, some class?"

"My mom's got this book. Gottman, some psychologist. He says a complaint's about a specific behavior and criticism's about the person's character. I didn't think it applied to basketball." He hesitated, because honesty cut both ways. "I'm not sure I'm doing it right, either. It might still stink to hear."

"It stinks a little," Marcus admitted. "But it stinks like something I can do something about." He put the free headphone back in his ear, then took it out again. "Tuesday. Show me the closing-out drill before warmups?"

"Before warmups," Eli agreed.

They walked out together through the lobby where the janitor was mopping, the smell of disinfectant sharp in the cool air. Eli thought about his biology teacher's obsession with speciation, how one population splits into two until they can't interbreed anymore, and how teams did that too, quietly, in the corners of gyms, one careless sentence at a time. Maybe that was dramatic. Probably it was. But at the door, Marcus held it open for him and said, "Tell Dara the corner thing. In those words."

"Four threes," Eli said. "In those words."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
story:
The video arrived at 11:40 on a Tuesday night, while Brayden sat cross-legged on Dex's bedroom floor with a physics problem set abandoned between them. It showed a warehouse fire, orange light boiling through broken windows, a caption claiming it was the food distribution plant outside their town, burning that very hour, arson suspected, share before they bury it. Dex's thumb hovered over the send arrow.

"Three hundred shares already," Dex said. "My cousin's a pundit about this stuff, he'll want it."

Brayden watched the flames a second time through. Something about the framing bothered him, the way the phone camera never shook. He had spent the whole semester metabolizing the fact that he'd forwarded a fake lockdown video in March, that his aunts had passed it on, that his little cousin's school had gotten panic calls over nothing. He'd apologized once, in a group chat, and the apology had felt evanescent, gone before anyone read it properly. He didn't want that again.

"Before you send it," he said, "check when that video first went up."

"It went up an hour ago. It says so."

"It says so." Brayden pulled out his phone. "The caption says so. The video doesn't."

Dex wanted, more than anything that semester, to be the guy who knew first. He ran the school's biggest anonymous gossip account, forty followers shy of two thousand, and breaking news was his currency. His whole body angled away from Brayden, toward the send arrow, the way a plant angles toward a window.

"Everyone's already sharing it," Dex said.

"So be the one who says it's old."

Brayden typed slowly, the physics problem forgotten. He remembered something from a thread he'd read months ago, about searching a picture instead of words. TinEye, it was called, a reverse image search engine that had launched in 2008. He'd never actually used it. He paused the video on its clearest frame, the fire against the skyline, and screenshotted it, then uploaded the screenshot and waited while the little wheel turned.

Dex leaned over despite himself. "What'd you find?"

Results. A page of them, the same warehouse, the same orange boil. Brayden's stomach dropped somewhere below the carpet. Then he saw the sorting option, clicked it, set it to oldest first, and the page rearranged itself. The earliest result was dated years before, from a shipping depot fire in another state entirely. The video wasn't an hour old. It was old footage wearing tonight's caption like a stolen coat.

"There it is," Brayden said, and turned the screen around.

Dex took the phone. He scrolled, and his face did something complicated, relief and loss fighting for the same territory. "You can sort it oldest first," he said. "That's how you find when it showed up the first time."

"That's how you find out somebody's lying to you."

"Or somebody got it wrong," Dex said, defensive now, because the account was his and so was the impulse. "Maybe the guy who posted it didn't know either."

"Maybe." Brayden let the word sit. He didn't actually know whether the original poster had lied or just believed the caption the way Dex had been about to. That part stayed dark, and he was tired of pretending otherwise. "But your two thousand followers don't need another maybe."

Dex typed a reply to the thread instead of a share. This video is from years ago, found it with a reverse search, don't forward it. His thumb hesitated over the post button the same way it had hesitated over the arrow. He pressed it.

They went back to the physics problem set, or pretended to. Twenty minutes later Dex's phone buzzed and buzzed again. The reply was spreading, screenshot and all, people thanking him, one comment saying this account actually does the work, and Dex held the phone up so Brayden could watch the follower count tick upward, past the two thousand he'd been chasing all semester. The correction had done what the rumor was supposed to do.

"Look at that," Dex said. "Being careful got me more followers than being first."

He refreshed the page again, and Brayden saw the new post already drafting itself in Dex's notes app, a formula now, busted and verified in bold, ready for the next fire. Outside, a car passed the house slowly, its headlights crawling across the ceiling and away, and somewhere in the group chats the warehouse video kept burning, older than anyone sending it, unstoppable as a rumor with a head start.

"Send me that screenshot," Brayden said, holding out his hand.

"Why, so you can check my checking?"

"So I can learn how to do it myself."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
story:
Logan had the kitchen table to himself for exactly forty minutes, which was the terms of the treaty. His sister Nadia wanted the oven at seven for a lemon cake, and to propitiate her he had already surrendered the last two cookies and wiped down the counter without being asked. In exchange he got the table, the good light from the window, and the electric kettle.

He spread out the lab write-up and the photocopied page with the reaction on it, the one where the forward direction drank in heat. His friend Marcus had texted him three times that afternoon about it. Their teacher had split the class into pairs to predict what would happen when the reaction was warmed, and Marcus insisted it would shift back toward the reactants, because heat was a product of everything, wasn't it, that was what he remembered from somewhere. Logan had said he wasn't so sure. The argument had felt seismic at lunch, the kind that makes you recheck your own handwriting, though now, alone with the page, it was only a question.

The page told him the forward reaction was endothermic. That word he trusted. Beyond that it said nothing helpful, just asked him to predict the shift when the temperature was raised. He could look up the answer, but Marcus had a habit of being loudly wrong in ways that made Logan doubt himself, and he wanted something better than a website. He wanted to see it.

Nadia came through in her socks, bowl under one arm. "Is that chemistry? You're doing chemistry where my cake goes?"

"Forty minutes. I scrubbed the stove."

"You scrubbed the stove to propitiate me. Fine." She set a stick of butter on the windowsill to soften and stayed to watch him, which was her way of claiming the room without admitting it.

Logan filled a glass from the tap and set it in a pot of warm water, then mixed the sample solutions the way the lab sheet described, the ones that turned the whole business pink when the products formed. The pink was faint, barely a blush in the cold glass. He slid the pot onto the burner and turned the dial low.

"Le Chatelier's principle," he said, mostly to himself. "That's what it's called. The thing we're supposed to be using."

"You're narrating now," Nadia said.

"I'm thinking out loud. If the forward reaction is endothermic, and we raise the temperature, which way does it shift?"

"Toward whatever likes the heat, obviously. The plants on the south side of the house."

"That's not chemistry, that's gardening."

"Everything is gardening if you do it right."

He watched the glass instead of answering her. The water in the pot moved in small uneasy circles. Marcus's version ran through his head again, shift toward the reactants, and Logan turned it over the way you turn over a coin you suspect is double-headed. Marcus wanted to be right more than he wanted to be correct; Logan knew that about him and knew, also, that this did not make him wrong. Wanting something was not evidence. He had learned that the hard way in eleventh grade about a girl named Renee, and it was strange how a principle could follow you around like that.

The pink deepened. It crept up through the solution the way dawn does through a curtain, not at once but undeniably, until the glass held a color that could not be argued with. Logan lifted it out with the tongs and held it against the window. Warmer, and the reaction had moved toward the products. He got his phone and took two pictures, then set the glass on a trivet to cool, and while he watched, slowly, the pink began to pale again as the solution lost its heat.

So Marcus had it backwards. Logan wrote it in the margin of the lab sheet in small letters so it would look like something he had known all along, then crossed that out and wrote it larger, plainly: if the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products. He would tell Marcus tomorrow before class, quietly, not at lunch in front of everyone, because Marcus turned into a bit of a misanthrope when he lost an argument in public, all shrugged shoulders and short answers for the rest of the day.

What Logan could not figure out, sitting there while Nadia preheated the oven and reclaimed her territory dish by dish, was why. The fact sat in his hand like a smooth stone he could not see through. Something about it worked, that much the glass had shown him, and something about it balanced, because the color went and came back with the heat. He understood the prediction and not the reason, and he let that be true for now rather than pretending otherwise.

He texted Marcus one line: got it wrong, come by before class, I'll show you the pictures. Then he pushed his papers into his bag, and Nadia slid her cake pan into the oven, and the kitchen began to smell like lemon.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
story:
Camille had failed the last quiz, and Mr. Ruiz had written one word beside her score, "see me," which she had no intention of doing. Instead she came early on Thursday to Room 114, where the smell of whiteboard marker still hung from the day before, and spread her homework across the lab bench: a problem about methane burning in oxygen, a periodic table with a coffee ring on it, and a page of arithmetic that collapsed every time she reached the third line.

The problem asked how many moles of water formed from 8.0 grams of methane reacting with 5.0 grams of oxygen. She had gotten as far as dividing 8.0 by 16.04 to find moles of methane, and there she stalled, because the oxygen sat in the corner of the problem like a door she hadn't tried.

"You're here early," said Priya, dropping her backpack on the neighboring stool. Priya had habituated herself to this room the way other people habituated themselves to a favorite chair, arriving at 7:20 every morning as if some private ordinance required it. Camille envied that certainty. Her own relationship to chemistry was more like a truce that kept breaking down.

"I'm trying to figure out why my answer was wrong," Camille said. "I got a number for water from the methane. But the quiz said that wasn't it."

"Did you check the oxygen?"

"Why would I check the oxygen? There's methane and there's oxygen and it makes water. The methane is the thing I'm counting from."

Priya pulled a paper bag out of her backpack and set it on the bench between them. Inside were two slices of bread, a block of cheese, and an apple. "My mom packs me sandwich ingredients because she thinks the cafeteria bread is stale. Watch." She laid out the bread, sliced the cheese into six pieces. "If I wanted to make sandwiches, how many could I make?"

"Two," Camille said. "You only have two slices."

"Right. Even though there's cheese for six. The bread runs out first, so it decides how many sandwiches I can actually make." Priya tapped the bread. "Same idea in your problem. Whatever runs out first is what caps the product."

Camille looked at her page. She found the molar mass of oxygen, 32.00, and divided 5.0 by it, and then divided the moles of methane by the moles of oxygen, and the ratio came out wrong, lopsided, one of them too small. "So one of them runs out before the other," she said slowly.

"Which one?"

"Oxygen. There isn't enough oxygen to burn all the methane." She wrote it in the margin: O2 runs out first. Then she worked forward from the oxygen instead of the methane, through the balanced equation, two moles of water for every mole of oxygen, and came out with a number smaller than her quiz answer. A different number entirely. "Is that it? That's the answer?"

"Try it," Priya said, already biting into an apple slice and the cheese together, breadless.

Camille checked it against the back of the textbook, and there it was, her exact figure, sitting in the answer key as though it had always been obvious. She sat back. She had spent two weeks believing the problem was arithmetic, and it had been something else the whole time: a question about which ingredient gave out. The realization was not triumphant exactly. It was quieter than that, and slightly annoying, the way it always was when a thing turned out to be simple in a direction she hadn't thought to look.

"So the one that runs out first," she said, "that's the limiting reactant?"

"Yeah," Priya said. "That's the word."

Camille wrote the term at the top of her page, then drew a small slice of bread beside it, so she would remember. There was still a portion of the homework she couldn't do, the percent yield problems at the end, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she didn't yet know what those were asking. But she copied the methane problem into her notebook a second time, from the beginning, doing every step herself without looking at the first attempt, and it came out the same. Twice now. She closed the notebook and slid it into her bag.

"Thanks," she said. "For the bread thing."

"You owe me a sandwich," Priya said, folding the bag closed. "And you still have to bring the bread."

The bell hadn't rung yet. Through the window over the sinks, the parking lot was filling with buses, their exhaust ghosting upward in the cold. Camille zipped her bag, then unzipped it and took out the notebook once more, opened it to the fresh page, and under the little drawing of the slice of bread wrote, in small letters, runs out first, then decides. She put the pen away and carried the notebook to first period in her hand instead of her bag, holding it like something that might still be needed.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
story:
The kettle ticked on the stove, and Evan held his phone above his head like a divining rod, beseeching the grandfather's router for one usable bar of signal. The router was in the hall closet, behind a box labeled TAXES 1987-1994, and it offered its password to no one. His grandfather came in from the garden with dirt under his nails and recited the password from memory, all sixteen characters, without once looking up from the tomatoes he was setting on the counter.

"Do the lessons offline," he said. "The internet only distracts you anyway. In my day we wrote things down and remembered them."

Evan had agreed to spend the week here partly for the quiet and partly because his mother had used the word bonding in a tone that allowed no appeal. He was taking an online course in databases because the community college let high schoolers in free, and because something in him wanted to know how systems knew things. His grandfather, once he understood what a database was, had produced from the bedroom a cloth-bound ledger, decades of his mail-order plant nursery customers, and another binder of their orders. "Then put me in it," he said. "If a machine can hold my customers, let it hold them properly."

So Evan spent the afternoons typing. Two tables took shape on the old laptop: one he called Customers, with names and towns his grandfather dictated over his shoulder, and one he called Orders, rows of catalog numbers and dates and the little totals, three forty-five, twelve dollars, that had once arrived in envelopes. His grandfather was an epicure about very few things, coffee chiefly and soil secondarily, but he had opinions about customer records too. "Mr. Halloran," he said, tapping the screen with a finger that left a smudge. "He ordered a plum tree in 1998 and nothing since. Your machine should know that about him. A man who ordered nothing for twenty years, that is worth knowing."

The lesson's exercise wanted exactly that: a list showing every customer and their orders, so you could see who had gone quiet. Evan wrote the query at the kitchen table while his grandfather roasted beets, and when he ran it the result came back with rows that made no sense to him. Names appeared with empty gaps beside them, gaps the screen labeled NULL. He counted them. He had expected a neat row of names each with its order beside it, and instead here were fourteen customers whose order columns showed nothing at all, not zero, not blank in the way a spreadsheet was blank, but this other word, capitalized, faintly accusatory. He wrote the exercise off as broken and went to help with the beets.

At dinner he explained the problem anyway, because his grandfather asked, and because the failure had been sitting in his chest all evening like a stone. Every customer should have been in the list, he said. That was the point of the exercise. Instead some rows came out mangled, showing names and then these NULL things where the orders belonged. His grandfather chewed, considered, and asked one question: "Which table did you put first?" Evan looked at him. "Customers," he said. "The customers table is on the left." He said it and then heard himself say it, and put his fork down. He had typed the words LEFT JOIN without ever once thinking about the left.

He cleared the plates and went back to the laptop and looked at what he had written, the word LEFT sitting there in his own query, patient as furniture. He swapped the tables in his head to see what would happen, imagined Orders on the left instead, and understood that the list would then show every order, and only those customers who happened to match one. He did not run that version. He sat with the two possible lists instead, one holding all his customers and one holding all their orders, and tried to decide which one a person would actually want, and found he could argue both ways. The customer list with its NULLs told you who had gone silent. The order list told you what had actually been bought. Neither one was the whole truth by itself.

He printed the customer list, because his grandfather distrusted screens for anything permanent, and carried it out to the porch where the old man was identifying rocks from a drawer of specimens with a magnifying glass, holding up something dark and speckled and declaring it igneous, born in fire, older than any of his customers. Evan set the paper on the rail. Fourteen names had NULL beside them, and at the top of that column, at the very top, was Mr. Halloran.

"Twenty years," his grandfather said, and reached for the phone.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
story:
The laundromat on Fenwick Street had one working folding table, and Levi had commandeered it before anyone else could claim it, spreading two leases side by side between the detergent and a stranger's abandoned sock. His mother would say he was being adult about this, which was her way of saying she wished his father were the one helping. He didn't call his father. He called the number on the lease for the Halloway Street apartment instead, because the lease said utilities weren't included and gave no hint what they might cost.

A woman came in while the phone was still ringing, towing a hamper with a bad wheel. She was maybe fifty, wearing a coat that suggested she'd dressed for a colder decade, and she looked at the table, at his papers, at him, and sat down two machines away without comment. Levi decided she was annoyed with him. He was probably taking up too much room.

"Halloway Property Management," said a man's voice.

"Hi, I'm looking at the one bedroom, and I'm trying to figure out what electricity actually runs there. Is there any way to know?" Levi had his pen uncapped, hovering over a blank space he'd drawn under the Halloway rent.

"I can tell you the previous tenant's typical usage. It ran about 600 kilowatt-hours a month."

"Sorry, what's that in dollars?"

"Depends on the rate. Around here it's about 15 cents a kilowatt-hour. So 600 at 15 cents each, call it 90 dollars a month. And that's before whatever fixed monthly charges the utility adds on, the account fee and such."

Levi wrote 90, then wrote before fixed charges underneath it, in smaller letters, because it felt like the kind of thing that would come back to bite him if he rounded it away. "Thanks. That's really helpful." He hung up and did the arithmetic again on his own, moving the decimal, multiplying, arriving at the same 90, and felt the small dumb pleasure of a number that held still.

The woman had migrated closer than he'd registered. "You're apartment hunting," she said. Not a question.

"Comparing two places. This one's cheaper on paper but doesn't include utilities. The other one's more rent but heat and water are in it." He hesitated, then turned the Halloway lease toward her, because explaining it to someone else was a way of testing whether he understood it himself. "So the rent is 780, and I've got maybe 90 for electricity, plus whatever that fixed charge turns out to be, plus internet, and I don't even know about that yet."

She squinted at the page. "The other one?"

"895 with heat and water included. So it's, like, 115 more in rent, but if electricity's 90 plus the fee, the gap's maybe 20 bucks. Basically nothing." Even as he said it, he heard the parts he was leaving out: the fixed charge he hadn't priced, the fact that the previous tenant's usage was the previous tenant's, not his. He'd lived his whole life in houses where the lights just worked, where the bill arrived and someone else paid it, and now the whole invisible system was itemizing itself in front of him.

"My son did this," the woman said. "Two years ago. He made a spreadsheet." She said "spreadsheet" the way an aesthete might say "motel," with a faint grief for what the world had come to, and Levi revised his earlier read of her entirely; she hadn't been annoyed, she'd been lonely, or at least she was now talking to him with no complaint about the table at all. "You know what he figured out in the end? He took the more expensive one because the windows were bigger."

"That's a terrible reason."

"It's what he could afford to care about then." She started loading her washer with a kind of ceremonial slowness, one garment at a time, like she was auditing them. The third machine from the wall sat moribund, its glass fogged, an OUT OF ORDER sign gone soft with age, and Levi realized he'd been sitting near it for twenty minutes without seeing it, which seemed like information about something, though he couldn't have said what.

He added the columns twice. Halloway, best case: 780, 90, a fixed fee he'd guess at 10, internet he'd guess at 45, so 925, plus the risk that the previous tenant ran a space heater all winter or nothing at all. The other place: 895, internet 45, so 940, with fewer ways to be surprised. They were close enough that the decision wasn't really about math anymore, and he didn't yet know what it was about. His first load had gone still in the dryer. He pulled the warm clothes into his arms, left the leases splayed on the table where she could look at them if she wanted, and said, "I'm going to go walk the block between the two buildings before I sign anything."

"Bigger windows," the woman called after him, and the dryer door clanged shut on her laughter.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
story:
The wifi at Grandma June's house came from a router older than Hailey, so she sat on the porch steps with her laptop, drafting the message she had been avoiding for four days. On the screen was a half-finished robotics notebook and, at the top of the messages app, Priya's name. Priya had missed the Friday deadline for the code documentation again, which meant Hailey had spent her whole Sunday writing it herself, which meant Hailey had opinions. The problem was that her opinions currently read, in her head, as something like "you're lazy and I hate carrying you," which she suspected would eviscerate their friendship without actually fixing anything.

Inside, Grandma June was playing solitaire with an actual deck of cards, because she distrusted computers the way some people distrust weather. Grandpa Walt, who lived two houses down and came by mostly to eat, was in his usual chair being a taciturn monument to the belief that most people were not worth talking to. Hailey sometimes thought he was a misanthrope the way other men were fishermen, practicing it steadily and with pride.

"When I was on the line at the plant," Grandpa said apropos of nothing, "foreman told me my welds were garbage. That was the whole speech." He turned a page of his newspaper. "Fifty years I'm still deciding if he was right."

"You remember one bad review for fifty years?" Hailey called through the screen door.

"I remember the bad ones. The good ones I made up myself." He went back to his paper, and Hailey sat with that for a moment, because it was a little terrifying. Whatever she sent Priya might be remembered for fifty years, or at least until graduation.

She had tried drafting the message twice already. The first draft was so nice it said nothing. The second was honest in the way a hammer is honest. Flashback: last semester, group project, Marcus turned in slides with clip art of actual cartoon frogs, and Hailey had said, in front of everyone, "This looks like a ten-year-old made it." The teacher had pulled her aside afterward and said something Hailey still turned over at odd hours, that cruelty and honesty were not the same thing and she should figure out which one she was doing. Marcus had laughed it off, but he also never sat near her again, and she had noticed, and it had bothered her in a low persistent way, like a stone in a shoe.

She typed "how to give feedback that isn't terrible" into the search bar, half expecting a listicle, and instead found something from the Center for Creative Leadership. She read it twice on the porch steps while a jay yelled at her from the fence. There was a name for it, and she said it out loud to test it: "The Situation-Behavior-Impact model." It framed feedback by naming three things: when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had. She looked at her two dead drafts and then back at the screen. Was the problem that she'd been trying to say everything at once, all of Priya, whole and forever lazy, instead of one Friday, one deadline, one consequence? That felt almost too simple. But simple and easy weren't the same thing, and this was not easy.

She tried the shape out on the message. When: Friday, the documentation deadline. Behavior: Priya hadn't turned in her section, and hadn't said she wasn't going to until Saturday. Impact: Hailey had written the documentation alone on Sunday and now felt like she couldn't trust the schedule, which made her want to stop sharing files with Priya at all. That last part was the scary part, the honest effect, because it admitted she'd been thinking about quietly taking over everything, which was its own kind of rudeness.

"It's not a compliment sandwich," she said to the jay, who did not care. It was more like pointing at the actual ground instead of at the horizon and yelling. Did it count as kind, though, if it was only specific? Kindness might be the specific part, actually. She wasn't sure, and she wrote that into the message too, at the end, that she didn't know how to say it better yet and was still figuring that out.

Grandma June appeared at the screen door with two glasses of lemonade and handed one through. "You've been muttering at that porch for an hour," she said. "Send it or don't."

Hailey deleted the frog-sentence she'd been tempted to open with, reread the message one last time, and pressed send. Then she carried her lemonade over and sat on the arm of Grandpa's chair, which he permitted without comment, and they watched the jay terrorize the fence together until her phone buzzed on the step behind them.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
story:
The library smelled of dry radiator heat and somebody's microwave noodles, and Violet had been staring at the same page for ten minutes. Her debate coach had assigned her the comparison nobody wanted: how a parliamentary system picks and drops a head of government, next to how a presidential one does it. The tournament was Friday. Her partner, Denis, slid into the chair across from her and dropped his binder on the table with a thud that made the boy at the next carrel look up.

"You have anything yet?" he said.

"I have a headache and three books that disagree with each other." She turned the binder so he could see her notes. "Here's the part I can't make clean. In a presidential system we elect the head of government directly, more or less, and we can only get rid of them through impeachment, which almost never works. In a parliamentary system the parliament picks the prime minister or chancellor, so it can also unpick them. But the books say some countries can't just vote no. Some of them have to vote yes on somebody else at the same time."

"Then say that."

"I can't just say that. I have to know whether it matters." She pulled the German constitution volume toward her again, the one with the cracked spine. "Mrs. Okafor will ask for an example. She always asks for an example."

Denis leaned back and laced his fingers behind his head. "Then find one."

The radiator ticked. Violet ran her finger down the index of the German volume, past headings about federalism and the Bundesrat, and stopped at a phrase she'd copied earlier without understanding: constructive vote of no confidence. She followed the reference to a paragraph in the middle of a chapter on the Bonn Republic, and read it twice, and felt the small cold jolt of a fact that rearranges everything around it.

"Denis. Listen to this." She kept her voice low, aware of the boy at the next carrel. "In 1982 Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence. And it's the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level."

"So it's a vote of no confidence," Denis said.

"No. It's a constructive vote of no confidence. That's what it's called. That's the whole point of the name." She was flipping back and forth between pages now, her pen moving. "They couldn't just throw Schmidt out. They had to choose Kohl at the same moment. The country woke up with a new chancellor and there was no general election at all."

Denis frowned at his own binder. "So the Germans changed leaders and nobody voted?"

"That's what I'm looking at."

He was quiet for a second. "That's going to sound terrible in the round. The other team will lambaste us for defending a system where the voters get skipped."

"Then maybe I shouldn't defend it." Violet wrote fast, crossing out her earlier outline. "Maybe the honest case is that both systems are protecting something, just different things. The presidential system protects the head of government from being removed by ordinary politics, so removal has to be this huge rare event. The parliamentary system protects the government from collapsing into nothing, because you can't say no without saying yes to somebody new." She stopped, hearing herself, and pressed the pen against her lip. "Except I don't actually know which protection matters more. That's the part I can't resolve."

"So leave it open."

"You can't leave a debate case open. Judges hate that."

"Judges hate fake certainty more." He tapped her page. "Say both systems trade one risk for another and you're not sanguine about either. You're allowed to be unsure, Violet. It's a comparison, not a cheer."

She wanted to argue with him, and the wanting was itself informative, because she recognized it as the same instinct the German provision seemed designed to frustrate: the desire to say no without having to say yes. If she tore up the parliamentary system in her conclusion, what was she offering instead? If she tore up the presidential one? She wrote a question mark in the margin, hard enough to tear the paper a little.

The bell for the passing period rang, and the boy at the next carrel packed his headphones away and left, and the library went quieter. Violet copied the 1982 fact onto a notecard, then copied it a second time because the first one was smudged. Under it she wrote, in smaller letters, only time at federal level, and then, after a pause, why only once? She didn't have an answer, and she underlined the question anyway.

At lunch she found Marisol from her civics class at the corner table by the window, where the sun made an oblong on the linoleum. Marisol's family had come from Lima, and she had opinions about constitutions the way other people had opinions about music.

"Guess what I found," Violet said, sitting down with her tray. "Germany. 1982. A chancellor got replaced with no election at all."

Marisol set down her fork. "By who?"

"Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt. Through a constructive vote of no confidence. It's the only time it's worked at the federal level."

"So one parliament, one afternoon, and the whole government changed." Marisol chewed on that, literally and otherwise. "Part of me thinks that's efficient. Part of me thinks the voters got robbed."

"That's exactly my problem," Violet said. She pulled the notecard out of her jacket pocket and set it on the table between their trays, the smudged one underneath, the clean one on top, the underlined question showing at the bottom edge. "I can argue both sides now. I just can't tell which one I actually believe."

Marisol picked up the card and held it to the light from the window. "Then argue both," she said, "and let the judges deal with it," and handed it back.
